1.summary: A switch is a hardware-based Layer 2 device that connects LAN devices and moves frames by MAC address, sending each received message only to the device it was meant for.
1.deeper:
A switch is hardware based and uses Application Specific Integrated Circuits (ASICs) to help make filtering decisions. It is a general connectivity component (aggregation point) that connects LAN components such as computers, printers and switches, and it is used for workgroup connectivity and network segmentation. It moves frames at the Data-Link Layer of the OSI model by reading the MAC address from the host's network interface card, and it transmits a received message only to the device it was intended for. Switches break up the network into collision domains.

Switch performance: hardware-based bridging; low latency; low cost, relatively inexpensive for the number of ports ("low-cost high port density"); and broadcast control: with VLANs, a switch can segment a network into smaller broadcast domains. Without VLANs, broadcasts are not filtered until they get to a Layer 3 device. Network interfaces (switch ports) are where end devices such as computers or printers connect.

Application Specific Integrated Circuits (ASICs): switches use them to build and maintain MAC address tables, and to learn, establish and manage numerous internal connections to pass or filter traffic.

Low latency: the switch can receive, process and apply an update in minimum time, resuming traffic flow quickly. In other words, switches are fast, and there is little lag on the network.

Console port: allows direct local access to configure a "blank" switch for the first time, from a terminal or a computer running terminal emulation software. DoD policy states the console port must be password protected to prevent unauthorized changes, because this local access only requires physical presence.
1.analogy: A switch is like a mail room for a building: special sorting machines (ASICs) read each address, mail moves with little delay, every office has its own slot, and a locked side door lets the manager set the room up.
1.scenario: An airman unboxes a blank switch and connects to its password-protected console port to configure it for the first time. Computers and printers then plug into its network interfaces. With VLANs set up, the switch segments the network into smaller broadcast domains, and its ASICs keep traffic moving with little lag.
1.example: A building's front desk sends each visitor straight to the right office instead of announcing them in every hallway. In the course: switches manage the flow of data across a network by only transmitting a received message to the device for which the message was intended, Block Text p.5.

1.summary: A MAC address is the 48-bit unique identifier of each networked device connected to a switch; the switch reads it to regulate traffic flow.
1.deeper:
Each networked device connected to a switch can be identified using a 48-bit unique identifier called a MAC address. A switch learns each connected physical device by that address. Switches move frames of information at the Data-Link Layer of the OSI model by reading the MAC address from the host's network interface card.

The MAC address allows the switch to regulate traffic flow: a switch transmits a received message only to the device it was intended for. This maximizes security, minimizes the bandwidth required and improves network efficiency. A hub, by contrast, provides no identification of connected devices. Switches use MAC addresses to make forward/filter decisions with Layer 2 frames, and the MAC address table pairs each learned address with the interface ID the device is connected on.
1.analogy: A MAC address is like the serial number stamped on each device: no two are the same, so the switch can always tell which device sent a frame and which device it is for.
1.scenario: Host A, Host B and Host C connect to a switch. Host A sends a frame for Host B. The switch reads Host A's MAC address from its network interface card and later sends frames for Host B only to Host B, because each host has its own unique MAC address.
1.example: Each house on a street has its own number, so a letter carrier can bring each letter to the right door. In the course: each networked device connected to a switch can be identified using a 48-bit unique identifier called a MAC address, Block Text p.5.

1.summary: A hub is a legacy device that copies a frame entering one interface out all of its other interfaces, so every connected device shares the bandwidth.
1.deeper:
Frames or messages that enter one interface on a hub get copied and repeated out all other interfaces, except the interface they originally entered. Hubs are legacy devices, less intelligent than a switch, but they are still found on various networks.

Hubs provide neither security nor identification of connected devices, so messages sent to a hub have to be transmitted out of every port. This greatly degrades the efficiency of the network, because the bandwidth is shared. A switch is considered more intelligent: it identifies each connected device by its MAC address and sends a received message only to the device it was intended for, and each switch port is a collision domain of its own because it does not share bandwidth.
1.analogy: A hub is like a person with a megaphone who repeats every message to the whole room, whoever it was meant for. A switch is like a messenger who walks each note to the one person named on it.
1.scenario: An airman finds an old hub still in use. When Host A sends a frame to Host C, the hub copies it out to Host B and Host C alike, because it cannot tell who is connected where. All three hosts share the bandwidth, which greatly degrades the efficiency of the network.
1.example: A building intercom that plays every call in every room interrupts everyone, even though each call is for one person. 1.summary: Random Access Memory (RAM) is the running memory a switch uses for all of its operations; configuration changes are stored there in the running-configuration.
1.deeper:
Internal components vary from switch to switch, but every switch has at least four in common: Flash Memory, Read Only Memory (ROM), Non-Volatile Random Access Memory (NVRAM) and Random Access Memory (RAM). RAM is the running memory the switch uses for all of its operations. Configuration changes made on the switch are stored in RAM, in a file called the running-configuration, which is used for operations.

Flash Memory: where the operating system (OS) is saved. Every time the switch boots up, flash memory is accessed to load the OS into the running memory.

Read Only Memory (ROM): contains the diagnostic and boot up routines.

Non-Volatile Random Access Memory (NVRAM): where the startup-configuration is saved, along with other information that needs long-term storage. At boot, NVRAM loads the startup-configuration into RAM.
1.analogy: A switch's memories are like an office. The filing cabinet (Flash Memory) keeps the manual, the safe (NVRAM) keeps the saved plan, the wall poster (ROM) shows the start-up routine, and the desk (RAM) is where the day's work is spread out and changed.
1.scenario: An airman powers on a switch. The OS is loaded from Flash Memory into RAM, and NVRAM loads the startup-configuration into RAM. The airman then makes a configuration change; it is held in RAM, in the running-configuration that the switch uses for its operations.
1.example: A desk is where papers are spread out and worked on during the day, while drawers keep what must last. In the course: RAM is the running memory that the switch uses for all of its operations, Block Text p.7.

1.summary: The startup-configuration is the configuration file saved in NVRAM for long-term storage; at boot it is loaded into RAM and becomes the running-configuration.

NVRAM is what is accessed to save the startup-configuration, along with other pieces of information that need long-term storage in the switch. The startup-configuration file is loaded to RAM upon boot up and becomes the running-configuration, with the entire configuration specific to that switch.

1.summary: Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) is a Data-Link layer protocol that establishes communication directly between two network devices over a point-to-point link, without relying on any host or network system.
1.deeper:
Point-to-Point Protocol establishes communication directly between two network devices without relying on any host or networking system. It is a data link layer protocol that operates over a point-to-point link: a link connecting two communicating link-level peers, one on each end of the link.

The PPP sender must take a network-level packet and frame (encapsulate) it within the PPP data link layer frame, so that the receiver can identify the start and end of both the data link frame and the network layer packet within it. PPP is one of the Layer 2 protocols named with STP, UDLD and CDP.
1.analogy: PPP is like two people at either end of a private line who put each message in an envelope marked where it begins and ends, so the person at the other end can take out exactly the message inside.
1.scenario: An airman connects two network devices with a single point-to-point link. PPP lets them talk directly, with no host or network system in between. The sender places each network packet inside a PPP frame, and the receiver finds the start and end of the frame and of the packet inside it.
1.example: A letter goes inside an envelope so it arrives whole and the reader knows where the letter starts and ends. In the course: Point-to-Point Protocol establishes communication directly between two network devices without relying on any host or networking system, Block Text p.7.

1.summary: Spanning Tree Protocol (STP), defined by IEEE 802.1D, is a Layer 2 loop-prevention protocol that lets switches find physical loops and build a loop-free logical topology.
1.deeper:
STP is a loop-prevention protocol that allows switches to communicate with each other in order to discover physical loops in a network. If a loop is found, STP specifies an algorithm that switches can use to create a loop-free logical topology. It prevents loops in Ethernet networks and ensures efficient and reliable data transmission, and it is the standardized solution for loop avoidance. In 2001 IEEE introduced 802.1w, the Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol.

IEEE 802.1D: the Ethernet MAC bridges standard, which includes bridging, the Spanning Tree Protocol and others. It is standardized by the IEEE 802.1 working group, and it defines STP.
1.analogy: STP is like park rangers who walk every trail, find where trails circle back on themselves, and close just enough gates that each spot can be reached one way only.
1.scenario: An airman's three switches are linked in a triangle for redundancy. The switches communicate with each other, discover the physical loop and use the STP algorithm. The result is a loop-free logical topology: frames no longer circle, while the physical links stay in place.
1.example: A one-way system in a car park keeps cars from circling back into each other. In the course: the Spanning Tree Protocol, defined by IEEE 802.1D, is a loop-prevention protocol that allows switches to communicate with each other in order to discover physical loops in a network, Block Text p.8.

1.summary: Unidirectional Link Detection (UDLD) detects links where traffic flows in only one direction and causes the switch that has trouble hearing to shut down its port.
1.deeper:
A unidirectional link occurs when traffic in one of two directions on a link fails. It could be caused by a bad transmitter, a bad receiver, a bad repeater or a bad cable segment. Only one device on the link will notice a problem.

This can cause a backup switch to not hear from its partner, to go into forwarding mode, and to create a switch loop, because its partner is still forwarding. UDLD causes the switch that is having trouble hearing to shut down the port, which prevents errors. Loopguard, named with it, instead puts the port into a new state: loop inconsistent state.
1.analogy: A unidirectional link is like a phone call where one side's microphone breaks: one person still talks, but cannot hear any answer. UDLD is the rule that the person who cannot hear hangs up, instead of acting as if the other side had left.
1.scenario: A cable segment between two switches goes bad, so traffic flows only one way: Transmit only, no receive. The backup switch stops hearing its partner and could go into forwarding mode while the partner is still forwarding, creating a switch loop. UDLD shuts down the port of the switch having trouble hearing, so the loop never forms.
1.example: A walkie-talkie that can send but not receive gives a false picture of the conversation, so its user should stop using it. In the course: UDLD causes the switch that is having trouble hearing to shut down the port, Block Text p.8.

1.summary: Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP) is an open, vendor-neutral IEEE-standard Layer 2 protocol that lets devices advertise data and Layer 2 configurations to their directly connected neighbors.
1.deeper:
LLDP is non-proprietary: an open IEEE-standard layer 2 protocol that runs over the data link layer for heterogeneous networks. It allows devices to advertise data and layer-2 configurations to their connected adjacent nodes. LLDP stores the MAC address, VLAN, IP management address, system names and other details, port details, MDI power and link aggregation, and advertises them to its neighbor. Being vendor neutral, it is commonly used as a component for network management purposes and network monitoring applications.

1.summary: Address learning is the switch function that learns the MAC address of every device connected to its ports, starting from an empty MAC address table.
1.deeper:
To function smoothly and securely, a Layer 2 switch must learn the MAC addresses of all devices connected to its ports. When the switch is first put into service, its MAC address table is empty. When any attached device transmits a frame, the switch takes the source address and places it in the table, along with the interface ID on which the device is connected.

The destination hardware address is not listed yet, so the frame is flooded (broadcast) out all active interfaces except the one it was received on: the switch learns where the destination is by flooding. When that device answers, the switch adds its MAC address and interface ID to the table. If the two computers now send frames to each other, the switch makes a point-to-point connection and forwards their frames only between the two. This continues until the switch knows all connected devices.

Address learning is one of the three basic functions of every Layer 2 switch, with the forward/filter decision and loop avoidance.
1.analogy: Address learning is like a new mail clerk with a blank list of desks. Each letter shows who sent it, so the clerk writes down the sender's desk. A letter for someone not on the list is called out to the whole floor; whoever answers gets written down too. Soon the clerk carries every letter straight to the right desk.
1.scenario: An airman puts a new switch into service. Host A sends its first frame, addressed to Host B. The switch writes Host A's MAC address and interface ID into its empty table, but Host B is not listed, so the frame goes out every other active port. Host B answers, and the switch adds Host B. From then on, frames between the two go only between their two ports.
1.example: At a new job, you learn a coworker's desk the first time they stop by, and until then you ask the whole office where someone sits. In the course: Address Learning learns the source MAC address when an attached device sends its first frame, Unit 1 Slides p.23.

1.summary: The MAC address table is the switch's list of MAC addresses and the interface IDs they are connected on; it starts empty and is used to forward and filter frames.
1.deeper:
Switches use ASICs to build and maintain MAC address tables, which help them make forwarding decisions. When a switch is first put into service, the table is empty. When an attached device transmits a frame, the switch takes the source address and places it in the table, along with the interface ID on which the device is connected. A frame for a destination that is not listed is flooded out all active interfaces except the one it came in on.

When a frame arrives, its destination hardware address is compared with this forward/filter MAC database; a listed destination is forwarded only out the interface identified with the host. Loops can make the table unstable: when copies of a frame arrive from more than one link, the table becomes confused about where a device is, and constant updating, called thrashing the MAC table, slows the network.
1.analogy: A MAC address table is like a seating chart a teacher fills in on the first day: each student who speaks up is written next to a seat number, and after that, notes are passed straight to the right seat.
1.scenario: An airman checks a switch that has just been put into service: its MAC address table is empty. Host A sends a frame. The switch writes Host A's source address next to the interface ID of port 1. When a frame later arrives for Host A, the switch finds it in the table and sends it only out port 1.
1.example: A coat check ticket pairs each coat with a numbered hook, so the right coat is found at once. In the course: the switch takes the source address and places it in the MAC address table along with the interface ID on which the device is connected, Block Text p.9.

1.summary: The forward/filter decision is the switch function that uses the MAC address table to send a frame only out the interface of its destination and keep it off every other port.
1.deeper:
The Layer 2 switch uses its MAC address table both to forward and to filter the frames it receives. When a frame arrives at a switch interface, its destination hardware address is compared to the forward/filter MAC database. If the destination is listed, the frame is forwarded only out the interface identified with that host and is not sent out any other interface: keeping it off the other ports is frame filtering. This helps fully utilize the bandwidth on all network segments attached to the switch.

If the destination is not listed, the switch floods the frame out all active ports except the one it came in on, as in address learning. Switches use MAC addresses to make forward/filter decisions with Layer 2 frames. The forward/filter decision is one of the three basic functions of every Layer 2 switch, with address learning and loop avoidance.
1.analogy: The forward/filter decision is like a receptionist with a staff directory. A visitor for someone listed is sent to that one office, and no other office is disturbed. A visitor for someone not listed is announced on every floor.
1.scenario: Host A sends a frame to Host B. The switch compares the destination hardware address with its MAC address table, finds Host B on port 2, and sends the frame only out port 2. Host C's port never sees the frame, so its bandwidth stays free for its own traffic.
1.example: A sorting office that puts each letter into only its own street's bag keeps the other bags light. In the course: if the destination hardware address is listed in the MAC address table, the frame is only forwarded out the interface identified with the host, Block Text p.10.

1.summary: Loop avoidance is the switch function that keeps the loops created by redundant links from repeating frames endlessly; the standardized solution is the Spanning Tree Protocol.
1.deeper:
A loop is simply having more than one path to a destination device. Loops are required: a switch can be a single point of failure in the network topology, and to overcome it, multiple links (paths) between switches or multiple switches are used. The resulting loops can cripple network-wide operation by endlessly repeating the retransmission of a frame. This causes instability in the switch's MAC address table, seen as broadcast storms, multiple frame copies and multiple loops.

Loops (redundant links) are necessary in a network, so the network is built to avoid their problems, and switches can be configured to avoid loops. IEEE standardized the solution, IEEE 802.1D, called the Spanning Tree Protocol (STP); in 2001 IEEE introduced 802.1w (Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol). Different types of spanning tree can be implemented to prevent loops.

Multiple loops: one of the biggest problems is multiple loops generating throughout an internetwork, meaning loops can occur within other loops, consuming bandwidth. If a broadcast storm were to occur, any usable bandwidth would be consumed and the network could not perform packet switching.
1.analogy: Loop avoidance is like a town with two bridges over a river. The second bridge keeps the town connected if one closes, but traffic signs must stop drivers from circling between the bridges forever.
1.scenario: An airman's two switches are joined by one link, a single point of failure. The airman adds links and a third switch so traffic has other paths. Now there are loops, and frames could repeat endlessly, so the switches run the Spanning Tree Protocol to keep a loop-free topology while the extra links stay in place.
1.example: A spare key keeps you from being locked out, but you still need to know where each key is. In the course: a loop is simply having more than one path to a destination device, Block Text p.10.

1.summary: A broadcast storm happens when nodes send broadcast data over a network link and other devices rebroadcast it back, until the whole network is overwhelmed and communication fails.
1.deeper:
Loops can make the MAC address table unstable, and that instability shows up as one of three problems: broadcast storms, multiple frame copies and multiple loops. In a broadcast storm, different nodes are sending broadcast data over a network link, and the other network devices are rebroadcasting the data back to the network link in response. The process eventually overwhelms the whole network and leads to the failure of network communication.

If loop avoidance schemes are not put in place, the switches flood (broadcast) endlessly throughout the internetwork. A storm consumes any usable bandwidth, and the network is no longer able to perform packet switching. There are many reasons a broadcast storm occurs, including poor technology, low port rate switches and improper network configurations.
1.analogy: A broadcast storm is like one person shouting a question in a crowded hall, and everyone who hears it shouting it back to the room. Each echo sets off more echoes, until the noise drowns out every conversation.
1.scenario: Three switches are joined in a loop, and no loop avoidance is in place. A host sends broadcast data. Each switch rebroadcasts it to the next, which sends it on again, around and around. The flood keeps growing until the whole network is overwhelmed and the airman's users cannot communicate at all.
1.example: When everyone in a large group chat replies to all, and then replies to the replies, the messages pile up until nobody can find anything useful. 1.summary: Multiple frame copies is a loop problem: a device receives copies of the same frame from different LAN segments at the same time, and the switch's MAC address table becomes confused.
1.deeper:
Multiple frame copies is one of the three problems loops can cause, with broadcast storms and multiple loops. Because a frame can arrive from different LAN segments at the same time, a device can receive multiple copies of the same frame of information.

The MAC address filter table becomes confused as to where a device (for example, a server or host X) is located, because the switch can receive the frame from more than one link. The switch may be unable to forward a frame because it is constantly updating the MAC filter table with source hardware address locations; this is called thrashing the MAC table, and the constant updating slows down the network. Loop avoidance prevents it.
1.analogy: Multiple frame copies is like getting the same letter through two mail slots at once: the clerk who tracks where each sender lives keeps crossing out and rewriting the sender's address, and has no time left to deliver mail.
1.scenario: Host X sends a frame. Because of a loop, copies of the frame reach Switch 3 over two LAN segments at the same time. Switch 3 sees Host X on one link, then the other, and keeps updating its MAC address table. While it thrashes the table, it may not forward the frame, and the airman's users notice the network slow down.

1.summary: Store-and-Forward switching stores the entire frame in internal memory and checks it for errors before forwarding it to its destination.
1.deeper:
Store-and-Forward switches store the entire frame in internal memory and check the frame for errors before forwarding it to its destination. Error checking is done with a CRC (Cyclic Redundancy Check), and a frame is discarded if an error is found. Store-and-Forward ensures a high level of error-free traffic, because bad frames are discarded instead of being sent across the network.

It is one of three switching methods, with Cut-Through and Fragment-Free. Each method has advantages and disadvantages, LAN switches are characterized by the forwarding method they support, and the method used depends on where the switch is in the network. Cut-Through copies only the destination MAC address and forwards bad frames; Fragment-Free, a hybrid, stores the first 64 bytes.

1.summary: Cut-Through switching copies only the destination MAC address into memory and sends the frame on at once, which reduces latency but forwards bad frames.
1.deeper:
Cut-Through switching copies only the destination MAC address into memory. The switch looks up the address in its switching table and places the frame on the outgoing interface. This reduces latency; however, bad frames are forwarded, and the destination ultimately has to request that the source send the frame again: the destination does the error checking. Cut-Through is used when speed is important.

It is one of three switching methods, each with advantages and disadvantages. Store-and-Forward stores the entire frame and checks it for errors before forwarding; Fragment-Free, a hybrid of the two, stores the first 64 bytes. No one switching technique works in every instance, and the method used depends on where the switch is in the network: Cut-Through works best at the core layer, where there are fewer errors and speed is important. Some switches use adaptive switching to select the best method based on traffic conditions.
1.analogy: Cut-Through is like a mail sorter who reads only the address on an envelope and drops it in the outgoing bin without opening it. Mail moves fast, but a damaged letter goes through too, and the person who gets it has to ask the sender for a new one.
1.scenario: An airman's switch sits at the core layer, where there are few errors and speed is important, so it uses Cut-Through switching. A frame arrives; the switch reads only the destination MAC address and sends the frame on. One frame has an error. The switch forwards it anyway, and the destination asks the source to send that frame again.
1.example: An express checkout lane is quick because the cashier skips some checks, so a mistake is caught only later at home. In the course: Cut-Through switching copies only the destination MAC address into memory, Block Text p.12.

1.summary: Fragment-Free switching is a hybrid of Store-and-Forward and Cut-Through: it stores the first 64 bytes of a frame before forwarding.
1.deeper:
Fragment-Free is the third of the three switching methods. It is a hybrid of Store-and-Forward and Cut-Through switching: it stores the first 64 bytes of a frame before forwarding. It checks only those 64 bytes because the first 64 bytes are where frame fragmentation is most likely to happen.

Its neighbours mark the two ends. Store-and-Forward stores the entire frame in memory and checks it for errors, discarding bad frames. Cut-Through copies only the destination MAC address into memory; it reduces latency, but bad frames are forwarded. No one switching technique works in every instance, and the method used depends on where the switch is in the network.
1.analogy: Fragment-Free is like a gate guard who checks only the first page of each delivery form, where most mistakes are made, and then waves the truck through. It sits between the guard who reads the whole form and the guard who reads only the address.

1.summary: A collision is the result when two system transmissions occur at the same time on shared bandwidth; collisions are a normal part of Ethernet communications.
1.deeper:
When two system transmissions occur at the same time, on shared bandwidth, the result is a collision. Collisions are a part of Ethernet communications and do not imply any error condition.

A late collision is like an Ethernet collision, except that it occurs after all hosts on the network should have been able to notice that a host was already transmitting. It shows that another system attempted to transmit after a host had transmitted at least the first 64 bytes of its frame. Late collisions are often caused by an Ethernet LAN that is too large and needs to be segmented, and also by faulty network devices on the segment and duplex mismatches (for example, half-duplex and full duplex) between connected devices.

Collision domain: the area where devices share bandwidth, so their transmissions can collide. A hub shares the bandwidth among all its devices. Switches break up the network into collision domains: each port on a switch is a collision domain because the port does not share bandwidth with other devices.
1.analogy: A collision is like two people on a shared radio channel who start talking at the same moment: their messages meet on the one channel they share, and nothing is broken. If someone keeps cutting in well after another has started, something is wrong with the channel or the people on it; that is the late collision.
1.scenario: An airman watches two hosts on a hub send frames at the same instant on the shared bandwidth: a collision, which is normal for Ethernet. Later the airman sees late collisions, where a host starts sending after another has sent its first 64 bytes. The airman checks whether the LAN is too large, whether a device is faulty, and whether two connected devices have a duplex mismatch.
1.example: Two cars reach a one-lane bridge at the same time and meet on it; nothing is broken, the lane is simply shared. In the course: when two system transmissions occur at the same time, on shared bandwidth, the result is a collision, Block Text p.13.

2.summary: A VLAN is a logical grouping of network devices into a single broadcast domain; it can span multiple switches, and communication between VLANs requires a Layer 3 routing process.
2.deeper:
Besides the forward or filter decision, switches can use VLANs to make sure network traffic stays local. With more network-intensive applications there can be too much traffic on a network, so an administrator must segment the network properly to keep problems on one segment from spreading through the internetwork. A VLAN is a logical grouping of network devices into a single broadcast domain, or flat network. VLANs limit broadcasts by keeping the broadcast from one VLAN from going to another VLAN, and because of that segmentation, communication between VLANs must go through a Layer 3 routing process.

VLANs can exist on a single switch or span multiple switches, such as Access Switches (ASWs) and Distribution Switches (DSWs). Cisco switches come with default VLAN 1 already created; after more VLANs are created, selected switch ports are assigned to each VLAN. VLANs are identified by a number, such as VLAN 1, VLAN 10 and VLAN 20, and that number is referenced in all systems: if VLAN 30 is created on one switch and on a connected switch, both treat all VLAN 30 traffic as a single local network.
2.analogy: VLANs are like teams in one large office: people sit wherever there is a desk, but each team has its own group chat. A message to the team reaches every team member and nobody else; to reach another team, the message has to be passed on by someone who links the two.
2.scenario: An airman's unit has users on two floors, each floor with its own switch. VLAN 10 is created on both switches for one workgroup and VLAN 20 for another. A VLAN 10 computer on the first floor and a VLAN 10 computer on the second floor share one broadcast domain; to reach a VLAN 20 computer, traffic goes through a router, a Layer 3 routing process.
2.example: A sports league can put players from different towns on one team, and they play together wherever they live. In the course: a VLAN is a logical grouping of network devices into a single broadcast domain, Block Text p.15.

2.summary: A broadcast domain is the group of devices that all see each broadcast packet one of them transmits; a flat network is a single broadcast domain.
2.deeper: Flat networks have a single broadcast domain, meaning that every connected device sees every broadcast packet that is transmitted. Every broadcast frame transmitted on a segment is seen by all devices on the segment, regardless of whether the device needs the data. A common example is a computer merely sending out a hello packet. In a small network this is not a problem, but when thousands of computers send out broadcast hello packets that all the connected computers see, bandwidth issues start. A VLAN is a logical grouping of network devices into a single broadcast domain: VLANs limit broadcasts by keeping the broadcast from one VLAN from going to another VLAN, so communication between VLANs must go through a Layer 3 routing process. A VLAN can span multiple physical LAN segments but keep the same, logical, broadcast domain.
2.analogy: A broadcast domain is like a hall where every announcement over the loudspeaker is heard by everyone in it. With a few people that is fine; with thousands all making announcements, nobody can get a word through. Splitting the crowd into separate rooms, each with its own loudspeaker, keeps each announcement in its own room.
2.scenario: An airman notices the network slowing as more computers are added. Every computer sends out broadcast hello packets, and in the flat network every connected computer sees every one of them. Grouping the computers into VLANs keeps each VLAN's broadcasts inside that VLAN, so each broadcast domain is smaller.
2.example: An announcement over a building's speakers is heard in every room, whether or not it concerns the people there. In the course: flat networks have a single broadcast domain, meaning that every connected device sees every broadcast packet that is transmitted, Block Text p.15.

2.summary: VLANs bring three benefits: increased security, flexibility and scalability, and no geographical barrier.
2.deeper: Increased security (who has access): every broadcast frame transmitted on a segment is seen by all devices on the segment, whether or not the device needs the data. With VLANs, security is increased because only the devices that are part of the same VLAN receive the frame, and the administrator controls each port and whatever resources it is allowed to use. Flexibility and scalability: VLANs add flexibility by limiting or adding only the devices you want in the broadcast domain, regardless of their physical location. No geographical barrier: with VLANs, workgroups are no longer confined to physical locations. A VLAN can span multiple physical LAN segments but have the same, logical, broadcast domain, so devices can be in different locations but communicate as if on the same network.
2.analogy: VLAN benefits are like moving a team from a shared open hall into its own group chat: outsiders no longer hear its messages, members can be added wherever they sit, and a member in another building is as close as one at the next desk.
2.scenario: An airman's workgroup is split between two buildings. With a VLAN, the members in both buildings share one broadcast domain and communicate as if on the same network, while devices outside the VLAN no longer receive the group's broadcast frames. When a new member joins from another location, only that device is added to the VLAN.
2.example: A conference call lets a team with members in different cities meet as if they sat in one room, and only invited people hear it. In the course: the VLAN benefits are increased security, flexibility and scalability, and removing geographical barrier limitations, Unit 2 Slides p.7.

2.summary: The default VLAN is VLAN 1: manufacturers configure switches with it, and every port is assigned to it until an administrator changes that.
2.deeper:
Switches are configured with default VLAN 1 by manufacturers; Cisco switches come with it already created. All ports are assigned to VLAN 1 automatically and stay there until the administrator changes them, and ports must be assigned membership to created VLANs. Ports should never be assigned to the default VLAN on any network, for security. Unused ports should be shut down and assigned to an inactive VLAN, to reduce vulnerabilities and improve security.

Switches also use VLAN 1 for in-band management and to communicate with other networking devices using Spanning-Tree Protocol (STP), Dynamic Trunking Protocol (DTP), VLAN Trunking Protocol (VTP) and Port Aggregation Protocol (PAgP), all untagged traffic. Because of this, VLAN 1 may unwisely span the entire network if it is not appropriately pruned, and if its scope is large enough, the risk of compromise can increase significantly. VLAN 1 should not be made the management VLAN.
2.analogy: The default VLAN is like the lobby of a new building: everyone who arrives starts out there until they are given an office. Nobody should be left working in the lobby, and rooms nobody uses are locked.
2.scenario: An airman sets up a new Cisco switch. Every port is already in VLAN 1, the default VLAN. The ports that users need are assigned to created VLANs, and the ports nobody uses are shut down and assigned to an inactive VLAN. No port is left in the default VLAN.
2.example: A new phone comes with factory settings that stay in place until its owner changes them. In the course: switches are configured with default VLAN 1 by manufacturers, Unit 2 Slides p.9.

2.summary: A trunk is a connection between network devices, typically switch to switch, that can carry more than one VLAN.
2.deeper:
A trunk, also known as a trunk link, is a connection between network devices that can carry more than one VLAN, typically from switch to switch. VLAN tags are applied to frames on a trunk to identify the individual VLANs, so trunks are also known as tagged ports; access ports, where end user devices are normally connected, are untagged ports. Without trunking, every VLAN would need a connection to every switch a user on that VLAN resides on, just to pass traffic: a switch with 15 VLANs would use 15 ports simply to pass VLAN traffic, which degrades the low-cost, high-port-density benefit of switches. With a trunk link, the traffic for all the VLANs passes over one link, or more when LACP or EtherChannel is used.

Inter-Switch Link (ISL): the Cisco proprietary standard for trunks, now deprecated. ISL also tags the frame, but instead of using the frame as it is, it adds a new header and trailer to the existing frame. ISL only works with Cisco devices.

IEEE 802.1q: the defined open standard for VLAN trunking. Unlike ISL, IEEE 802.1q works with all major manufacturers' models.
2.analogy: A trunk is like a highway between two towns that carries traffic for many neighbourhoods at once, instead of a separate road for each neighbourhood. Each car shows which neighbourhood it is going to.
2.scenario: An airman links two switches that each have users in the Sales, Marketing and Research VLANs. Rather than using one port per VLAN on each switch, the airman joins them with one trunk. The switches come from different manufacturers, so the trunk uses IEEE 802.1q, the open standard, not ISL, which only works with Cisco devices.
2.example: A multi-lane highway carries cars bound for many different towns over one road. In the course: a trunk is a connection between network devices that can carry more than one VLAN, Block Text p.18.

2.summary: Frame tagging uniquely assigns a user-defined trunking ID to each frame, so a switch can match the frame to the VLAN its traffic belongs to.
2.deeper: Frame tagging, also called frame identification or encapsulation, uniquely assigns a user-defined trunking ID to each frame. The trunking ID matches the VLAN to the traffic belonging to that VLAN. When an Ethernet frame crosses a trunk, a VLAN tag is applied; this keeps track of frames traversing a switch fabric. For example, the Sales VLAN is tag 10, the Marketing VLAN tag 20 and the Research VLAN tag 30. The switch examines this frame identifier to determine the frame's VLAN destination. When the frame is placed on an access port, a port that is a member of only one VLAN, the tag is removed. ISL, a trunking method, also tags the frame, but instead of using the frame as it is, ISL adds a new header and trailer to the existing frame.
2.analogy: Frame tagging is like a coloured luggage tag at an airport: on the shared conveyor the tag says which flight each bag belongs to, and the tag comes off when the bag reaches its owner.
2.scenario: A computer in the Marketing VLAN sends a frame to another Marketing computer on a second switch. As the frame crosses the trunk between the switches, a VLAN tag with trunking ID 20 is applied. The second switch examines the tag, finds the frame belongs to the Marketing VLAN, and places it on the Marketing access port, where the tag is removed.
2.example: A routing label on a parcel tells each sorting center where the parcel belongs, and it is thrown away once the parcel arrives. In the course: frame tagging uniquely assigns a user-defined trunking ID to each frame, Block Text p.18.

2.summary: An access port is a switch port that is a member of only one VLAN; it is normally where end user devices are connected.

2.summary: The management VLAN carries management traffic such as Telnet, SSH, SNMP and syslog and has an IP address for remote access by an administrator; it should never be VLAN 1.
2.deeper: The management VLAN is used for purposes such as Telnet (logging on to a computer), SSH, Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP), to manage and monitor network devices, and syslog, network devices sending messages to a logging server. It is assigned an IP address for remote access by an administrator. The management VLAN should never be assigned to VLAN 1. VLAN 1 is the default VLAN: switches use it for in-band management and to communicate with other networking devices using Spanning-Tree Protocol (STP), Dynamic Trunking Protocol (DTP), VLAN Trunking Protocol (VTP) and Port Aggregation Protocol (PAgP), all untagged traffic. So VLAN 1 may unwisely span the entire network if not appropriately pruned, and a large scope can increase the risk of compromise significantly. Best practices are to prune unnecessary ports from gaining access to VLAN 1 as well as the management VLAN, and to separate in-band management, device protocol and data traffic.
2.analogy: The management VLAN is like a staff-only corridor in a building: the people who run the building use it to reach the rooms they look after, and it is kept apart from the main hallway everyone else shares.
2.scenario: An airman needs to log on to a switch remotely and to collect its syslog messages on a logging server. The switch's management VLAN has an IP address for that remote access. Because VLAN 1 already carries untagged device protocol traffic and may span the whole network, the management VLAN is not VLAN 1.
2.example: A building manager has a separate phone line for maintenance calls, apart from the lines the tenants use. In the course: the management VLAN is used for Telnet, SSH, SNMP, and Syslog, Unit 2 Slides p.17.

3.summary: A router is a Layer 3 networking device that uses IP addressing to forward packets between networks.
3.deeper:
A router connects two or more lines from different networks. When a packet comes into a router, the router reads the IP address to determine the destination network, then uses the information in its routing table or routing policy to direct the packet to its next destination. Routers break up broadcast domains: each port on a router is a different network, and broadcasts stop at the router. A router's components are external or internal; the internal components and memory hierarchy (ROM, flash memory, NVRAM and RAM) are the same as a switch's. The external components are the physical connections: most routers include a console port, an auxiliary port and network interfaces. The console port allows you to configure the router locally with a computer running terminal emulation software; neither the port nor the router must be configured to use it, so it is where you connect to configure a blank router.

Auxiliary port: it allows you to configure the router remotely using a modem. It must be configured before you can use it, through the console port or any of the network interfaces. You will probably not use it in the field, and it should be disabled for security reasons.

Network interfaces: they are located on the motherboard or on separate interface modules, and a router can be configured over any of them. Ethernet (or Token Ring) interfaces are configured to connect to a LAN; synchronous serial interfaces are configured to connect to WANs.
3.analogy: A router is like a post office sorting desk at the edge of town: it reads the town on each envelope and sends it toward that town, never letting a local flyer leave the neighborhood.
3.scenario: An airman unboxes a blank router. The airman connects a computer running terminal emulation to the console port for the first setup, cables an Ethernet interface to the LAN switch and a serial interface to the WAN link, and leaves the auxiliary port disabled for security.
3.example: A mail sorter reads the town on each letter and puts it in the bag for that town. In the course: A router is a Layer 3 networking device that uses IP addressing to forward packets between networks, Block Text p.22.

3.summary: An internetwork is two or more different networks joined by routers: a router connects lines from different networks, so packets can travel from one network to another.
3.deeper: A router connects two or more lines from different networks, and routers in different networks can be connected to create an internetwork. Routers work primarily at Layer 3 (the Network Layer) and provide the routing functions that enable multiple networks to be combined into an internetwork; they do this through logical addressing. Implementing a functional internetwork is a complex undertaking, and four common internetworking challenges must be addressed. Connectivity: support communication between very different technologies, since different sites may use different types of media or operate at varying speeds. Reliable service: users and whole organizations depend on consistent, reliable access to network resources. Network management: centralized support and troubleshooting, with fault, configuration, accounting, performance and security issues addressed. Flexibility: room for network expansion or contraction and for new applications and services. Routers and switches are two of the primary devices used to overcome some of these challenges.
3.analogy: An internetwork is like several towns joined by crossroads. Each town keeps its own streets, and the crossroads let a traveler pass from one town into the next.
3.scenario: An airman's base joins two sites: one site's network uses different media and runs at a different speed than the other's. Routers connect the two networks into one internetwork. The airman still has to keep access to resources reliable, give the help desk centralized troubleshooting, and leave room to add a new service later.
3.example: Separate neighborhoods become one city once roads join them, yet each neighborhood keeps its own streets. In the course: Routers in different networks can be connected to create an internetwork, Block Text p.22.

3.summary: Gateway is a traditional name for a router that performs routing functions between networks; in today's terminology it often means a device that converts data from one protocol or format to another.
3.deeper: Internet routing devices traditionally have been called gateways, and historically the term named functions performed by today's routers. Within the routing world, a gateway refers to routers that perform routing protocol functions between machines or networks; such gateways may be within or between autonomous systems, and in this sense the term is synonymous with router. Gateways are also named by where they work: interior gateway routers move information within an autonomous system, exterior gateway routers move it between autonomous systems, and a default gateway serves as an access point to and from a specific subnet or network. In today's terminology, the term gateway often refers to a device that converts information or data from one protocol or format to another, such as when a device transmits a packet with TCP/IP to a destination using the IPX/SPX stack.
3.analogy: The word gateway is like the word "carriage": it once named one thing and is now often used for another, so the context tells you which is meant.
3.scenario: An airman reads an older document that calls the base routers gateways: it means routers that perform routing protocol functions between networks. A newer document uses gateway for a device that passes data from a TCP/IP host to a host using the IPX/SPX stack: it means a device that converts data from one protocol to another.
3.example: A translator who turns a letter in one language into another lets two people who share no language exchange messages. 3.summary: An autonomous system (AS) is a connected group of one or more IP prefixes run by one or more network operators with a single, clearly defined routing policy, such as the internal networks of an Air Force base.
3.deeper: RFC 1930 defines the autonomous system. An example is the internal networks within an Air Force base. An AS is a collection of networks under a common administration that share a common routing strategy, and it is the largest entity in the OSPF hierarchy. An AS can be divided into several areas, which are groups of contiguous networks and attached hosts. Routers with interfaces in more than one area are called area border routers. Interior gateway protocols route information within an AS; routing from one Air Force base to another is routing between autonomous systems, done by an exterior gateway protocol such as Border Gateway Protocol (BGP). Autonomous systems are assigned specific numbers for use in BGP routing.
3.analogy: An autonomous system is like one household with its own house rules: the rooms (areas) all follow those rules, and dealing with the house next door follows a different set of arrangements.
3.scenario: An airman maps the networks of a base. All of them are run under one clearly defined routing policy, so together they form one autonomous system. The airman divides it into areas of contiguous networks, and notes that traffic to another base leaves this AS and is routed between autonomous systems.
3.example: A school district runs many schools under one set of rules, while a neighbouring district has its own. In the course: an Autonomous System is a connected group of one or more IP prefixes run by one or more network operators which has a single and clearly defined routing policy, Block Text p.24.

3.summary: Interior gateway protocols (IGPs) route information between routers within one autonomous system, such as one Air Force base; RIP, OSPF and EIGRP are the common ones.
3.deeper: Interior gateway routers exchange information within autonomous systems and use a variety of interior gateway protocols to do it. Common examples are Routing Information Protocol (RIP), Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (IGRP), Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) and Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP). The most common interior gateway routing protocols are based on a distance vector algorithm (RIP), a link state algorithm (OSPF), or a balanced hybrid of the two algorithm types (EIGRP). When communication is required between autonomous systems, an exterior gateway protocol such as Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) is used instead.
3.analogy: Interior gateway protocols are like the house rules for moving around inside one home; different families may use different rules inside their own homes, while travel between homes follows the rules of the road.
3.scenario: An airman lists the routing protocols on a base. RIP, OSPF and EIGRP all exchange routes between routers inside the base's autonomous system, so they are interior gateway protocols. The link to another base runs BGP, an exterior gateway protocol.
3.example: A building's internal phone extensions connect the offices inside it, while outside calls go through the public network. In the course: Interior Gateway Protocols are those designed to route information within an Autonomous System, Block Text p.39.

3.summary: A default gateway is the IP address of the nearest router interface on a host's subnet, set on the host so it has a path to leave its LAN for a remote network.
3.deeper: A default gateway (router) is an IP address on a Layer 3 network device that serves as an access point to or from a network. The term also refers to a setting configured on hosts that gives them a path to leave a LAN, so they may transmit traffic to a remote network. The default gateway address is the nearest router interface on a subnet: a host uses the IP address of the router interface associated with its own subnet. When a host finds that a packet is addressed to a host on a different network, it uses the router's address, usually from the router's designation as the default gateway for the LAN, and sends an ARP request to learn that router interface's MAC address, unless the MAC address is already in its ARP cache. A default gateway is a host setting; a default route, the gateway of last resort, is a route inside a router.
3.analogy: A default gateway is like the main door of a building: anyone heading somewhere outside the building leaves through that door, the one nearest their own floor.
3.scenario: An airman sets up a computer on Subnet A. Its traffic to a remote network has to leave the LAN, so the airman sets its default gateway to the IP address of the router interface on Subnet A, not the router interface on Subnet B.
3.example: A letter for another town goes into the local mailbox on your own street, not a mailbox in another neighbourhood. In the course: the default gateway address is the nearest router interface on a subnet, Block Text p.25.

3.summary: A protocol is a formal set of rules and conventions that governs how computers and other network entities exchange information over a network medium.
3.deeper:
Actual communication across an internetwork is made possible by communication protocols. A protocol implements the functions of one or more of the layers of the OSI model. The Internet protocols, also called the TCP/IP protocol suite, are the world's most popular open-system (nonproprietary) protocol suite: they can be used to communicate across any set of interconnected networks and are equally well suited for LAN and WAN communications. The two best known are the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) and the Internet Protocol (IP). Besides lower-layer protocols such as TCP and IP, the suite also specifies common applications such as electronic mail, terminal emulation and file transfer.

Transmission Control Protocol (TCP): along with IP, one of the two best-known Internet protocols. BGP supports reliable updates by using TCP for acknowledgments of its update messages: the network administrator initiates a TCP connection-oriented session between neighbor routers, and BGP uses periodic keep-alives to maintain TCP connectivity.
3.analogy: A protocol is like the rules of a card game: every player must follow the same rules, or the game falls apart. A suite is a box of games that come with a shared rule book.
3.scenario: An airman's workstation sends electronic mail to a server at another base. Both machines follow the rules of the TCP/IP suite, so the message can cross a LAN and a WAN between them. If either side used rules the other did not know, no information would be exchanged.
3.example: Two people can only hold a conversation if they speak the same language and take turns. In the course: a protocol is a formal set of rules and conventions that governs how computers and other network entities exchange information over a network medium, Block Text p.27.

3.summary: The physical or MAC address is used to send information from one Layer 2 interface to another Layer 2 interface; each interface is identified by a unique 48-bit address.
3.deeper: Hosts generally have only one physical network connection, and so only one MAC address. Routers and other internetworking devices typically have multiple physical network connections, and so multiple MAC addresses, one on each interface. Each interface on a router is a separate collision domain and a separate broadcast domain. The second addressing type is the network or logical address, used at Layer 3 to send information from one network to another; IPv4 and IPv6 are types of logical addresses. Logical addresses usually exist within a hierarchical address space, are not permanent to a device, and are typically based on network characteristics such as a segment or VLAN. As a packet moves through an internetwork, its Layer 2 (MAC) addresses change, but its Network Layer (IP) addresses stay the same.
3.analogy: A MAC address is like the number painted on one loading dock: it gets a delivery from one dock to the next. The network address is like the city and street on the parcel, which say which place the parcel is finally going to.
3.scenario: An airman counts addresses in a small network. Each workstation has one physical connection and one MAC address. The router has three interfaces, so it has three MAC addresses, and each of its interfaces is its own collision domain and broadcast domain.
3.example: Each door in an office corridor has its own room number, so a note can be carried from one door to the next one. In the course: the physical or MAC address is used to send information from one Layer 2 interface to another Layer 2 interface, Block Text p.28.

3.summary: Path determination is when a router determines the optimal path (network) for a packet to travel.
3.deeper: Routers communicate with one another as part of path determination, and they build and maintain their routing tables through a variety of messages. A broadcast (routing update message) generally sends a whole routing table to all directly connected neighbor routers; by analyzing these updates, a router can build a routing table to the next hop to a destination. A multicast (link state advertisement) informs other routers of the state of the sender's links, and that link information can build a complete, detailed picture of the network's topology. Whichever method is used, the goal is a routing table with a way of reaching all available destinations. Routing involves two basic activities: path determination and packet switching. The transport of packets through an internetwork is relatively straightforward; path determination is where complexity comes into the process. Routers use routing tables to determine the best path, and routing protocols are responsible for both path determination and packet switching.
3.analogy: Path determination is the trip planning before a drive: comparing roads and picking the best one. Packet switching is the driving itself, junction by junction.
3.scenario: A router hears routing update messages from its directly connected neighbors. From them it works out which way leads to each network and writes the best next hop into its routing table. When a packet arrives later, the hard part, choosing the path, is already done.
3.example: A navigation app picks the best road to a friend's house before the car moves. In the course: Path Determination is when a router determines the optimal path (network) for a packet to travel, Block Text p.28.

3.summary: A link state advertisement (LSA) is a multicast message sent between routers throughout the network to inform other routers of the state of the sender's links.
3.deeper:
Link information from LSAs can be used to build a complete, detailed picture of the network's topology, so routers can determine the best routes to all network destinations. Link state protocols use multicast messaging for their routing updates. When routers receive an LSA, they copy the information for their own use and immediately resend the message through their other interfaces, which allows very fast convergence. Only the directly affected routers generate the message, and all routers receiving it are assured that the information is valid. Compare a broadcast routing update message, which generally sends a whole routing table to all directly connected neighbor routers.

Link State Advertisements (LSAs) in OSPF: interface information, the metrics used and other variables are included in OSPF's LSAs. The topology table contains the collection of LSAs received from all routers in the same area, and from that table each router calculates a shortest-path tree that yields its routing table entries.
3.analogy: An LSA is like a neighbor who notices a road closed outside their own house and phones it in to everyone on the block; each listener notes it and passes it on right away.
3.scenario: One router's link goes down. That router, and only that router, sends a link state advertisement by multicast. Each router that receives it copies the news for its own use and immediately sends it out its other interfaces, so the whole area learns of the change quickly.
3.example: When a store changes its own opening hours, it posts the notice itself, and the people who see it pass it on. In the course: a link state advertisement informs other routers of the state of the sender's links, Block Text p.29.

3.summary: Packet switching is the router function of forwarding a packet from router interface to router interface; the source and destination MAC addresses change as the packet travels, while the IP source and destination stay the same.
3.deeper: In most cases a host determines that the packet it is sending is addressed to a host on a different network. The host acquires a router's IP address, usually because the router is the default gateway for the LAN, and sends an ARP request to learn the router interface MAC address; if that address is already in its ARP cache, no ARP request is needed. The host then sends the packet addressed to the router port MAC address (in the Layer 2 header) with the Network Layer address of the destination host (in the Layer 3 header). The router receives the packet on its inbound interface and examines the destination Network Layer address. If it does not know how to forward the packet to the next hop, it usually discards it. If it does, it changes the source MAC address to that of its outbound interface and the destination MAC address to the next hop's input interface, and transmits the packet. The next hop may be the destination host; if not, it is usually another router, which makes the same switching decision. Compared with path determination, the transport of packets is relatively straightforward.
3.analogy: Packet switching is like a parcel handed between depots: each depot puts a new local delivery label on the box for the next leg, but the final street address on the box never changes.
3.scenario: An airman's workstation sends a packet to a server on another network. The workstation already has the router interface MAC address in its ARP cache, so it sends the packet straight to the router port. The router examines the destination network address, puts new source and destination MAC addresses on it, and passes it to the next hop.
3.example: A relay team passes a baton from runner to runner; the runner changes at each hand-off, but the finish line stays the same. In the course: packet switching is forwarding the packet from router interface to router interface, Unit 3 Slides p.22.

3.summary: The Internet Protocol (IP) is the primary routed Network Layer protocol of the Internet protocol suite: it gives connectionless, best-effort packet delivery and fragments and reassembles packets to fit each link.
3.deeper:
IP is a Network Layer protocol that contains addressing information and some control information that enables packets to be routed; along with TCP, it represents the heart of the Internet protocols, and it comes in IPv4 and IPv6. IP has two primary responsibilities: providing connectionless, best-effort delivery of packets through an internetwork based on logically assigned addresses, and providing fragmentation and reassembly of packets to support data links with different maximum-transmission unit (MTU) sizes. A packet sometimes has to be broken down so that it does not exceed the maximum message size of the network it is being sent across. IP breaks the message into smaller pieces and attaches an IP header to each, duplicating the information from the original header. Each piece is given a new calculated message offset, inserted in its IP header, and a new checksum is calculated for each fragment before the fragments are transmitted. At the receiving computer, the common identifier number groups the pieces and the offsets put them in the correct order; if the receiving computer does not allow sufficient buffer space for the full message, the data may be destroyed.

Time to Live: the IPv4 header carries a time to live (TTL) counter. If a packet's TTL counter expires while it is being routed through the network, the packet is discarded. A packet is also discarded automatically if the version number in its header is wrong.
3.analogy: IP fragmentation is like moving a long sofa through a narrow door in labelled pieces: each piece carries the same address and a number saying where it fits, so the pieces can be put back together in order at the other end.
3.scenario: An airman's computer sends a packet that is too large for the next network's maximum message size. IP breaks it into smaller pieces, gives each an IP header with a new offset and a new checksum, and transmits them. The receiving computer groups the pieces by their common identifier and uses the offsets to put them back in order.
3.example: A long book shipped in several boxes, each labelled with the same order number and a box number, can be unpacked in the right order. In the course: IP has two primary responsibilities, providing connectionless, best-effort delivery of packets and providing fragmentation and reassembly of packets, Block Text p.31.

3.summary: Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) maps a known IP network address to a MAC address by broadcasting a request on the LAN segment.
3.deeper:
ARP works within the Data Link and Network Layers, and many protocol suites implement it. On a single LAN segment, address resolution begins when a source host knows the IP address of a destination host but not its MAC address. An ARP request is broadcast into the LAN; every device on the segment receives and processes it, but only the host with the destination IP address replies. The ARP reply, holding that host's MAC address, is sent only to the source host. The destination MAC address is then placed in the Layer 2 header and the frame is transmitted.

When the destination is on a different LAN behind a router, the router (the default gateway) also receives the broadcast. Acting as a proxy, it checks its routing table, finds the remote host on another LAN and replies with its own MAC address, as if that address belonged to the destination host. The source then sends its frames for that host straight to the router, which forwards them.

ARP Cache: when a network address is successfully associated with a MAC address, the device stores the match in memory called the ARP cache. Whenever the source host communicates with that destination again, it checks its ARP cache and finds the MAC address, so it needs no new ARP request.
3.analogy: ARP is like calling out a name in a crowded room: everyone hears the call, but only the person with that name answers, and only to the caller. The caller then writes the answer in a notebook, the ARP cache, so the next time there is no need to call out again.
3.scenario: An airman's computer has the IP address of a printer on the same LAN but not its MAC address. It broadcasts an ARP request; every device on the segment processes it, and only the printer replies, straight back to the computer. The computer keeps the printer's MAC address in its ARP cache, so its later frames to the printer go out without asking again.
3.example: Someone who knows a colleague's desk number but not where the desk is asks the whole office, and only that colleague points the way. In the course: Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) is the process of mapping IP network addresses to MAC addresses, Block Text p.32.

3.summary: The hello protocol lets network devices learn the MAC and Network Layer addresses of other devices and identify their neighbors; its messages, sent at intervals, also show that a connected router still works.
3.deeper:
Various routing protocols employ a Network Layer hello protocol. Each hello packet contains the Data Link and Network Layer addresses of the sending device. After a router is powered up and assured that its interfaces are functioning, it uses the OSPF hello protocol to acquire neighbors: routers with interfaces to a common network. It sends hello packets to its neighbors and receives their hello packets. Hello messages are also sent at specific intervals as a keep-alive, letting routers know that the neighbor router and the link between them are still functional. In EIGRP, a neighbor's hello packet advertises a hold time, the time a router treats that neighbor as reachable and operational; if no hello arrives within the hold time, DUAL FSM is informed of the topology change.

Neighbor Discovery: the hello protocol enables network devices to identify one another through a process called neighbor discovery.

Neighbor Table: when a router discovers a new neighbor, it records the neighbor's address and interface as an entry in the neighbor table. In EIGRP, one neighbor table exists for each protocol stack supported.
3.analogy: The hello protocol is like new neighbours knocking on each other's doors to introduce themselves and write down each other's names, then waving every morning to show they are still there.
3.scenario: An airman powers up a router whose interfaces come up. It sends hello packets onto its networks and receives hellos back, so it discovers its neighbors and writes each one's address and interface into its neighbor table. From then on, regular hellos show each neighbor and link are still working.
3.example: Two radio operators check in with each other at set times; a missed check-in tells each that something may be wrong. In the course: hello messages are also sent at specific intervals to act as a keep-alive to ensure a connected router is still functional, Block Text p.32.

3.summary: The Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) is a Network Layer management protocol that reports errors and other information about IP packet processing back to the packet's source.
3.deeper: IP routing moves packets one hop at a time, and each router's part is limited to forwarding packets based on internal information. The routers do not monitor whether the packets get to their destination, and IP does not provide error reporting back to the source when routing anomalies occur: that task is left to ICMP. ICMP provides message packets to report errors and other information regarding IP packet processing back to the source, and it can be used to monitor packets for destination arrival. Its useful messages include Destination Unreachable, Time Exceeded, Router Advertisement, Router Solicitation, and Echo Request and Echo Reply, known as Packet Internet Groper (PING).
3.analogy: ICMP is like a delivery service's "could not deliver" notice: the parcel service itself just carries parcels, and the notice is what tells the sender something went wrong.
3.scenario: An airman's computer sends packets to a server, but a router along the way cannot deliver them. IP itself does not provide error reporting back to the source; that task is left to ICMP, which reports errors about IP packet processing back to the computer.
3.example: A returned letter stamped "address unknown" tells the sender that delivery failed. In the course: ICMP is a Network Layer Internet management protocol that provides message packets to report errors and other information regarding IP packet processing back to the source, Block Text p.33.

3.summary: Ping (Packet Internet Groper) tests IP through the network: it sends an ICMP echo request to a destination IP address, and a destination that receives it responds with an ICMP echo reply.
3.deeper: Ping is built on ICMP, the Network Layer Internet management protocol that provides message packets to report errors and other information regarding IP packet processing back to the source. ICMP generates several kinds of messages, including Destination Unreachable, Time Exceeded, Router Advertisement, Router Solicitation, and Echo Request and Echo Reply, which together are known as ping. A ping is a Network Layer to Network Layer test: it does not check the entire protocol stack. Routers do not monitor whether packets get to their destination, and IP does not report routing anomalies back to the source; that task is left to ICMP.
3.analogy: Ping is like calling out "Can you hear me?" across a field and waiting for "Yes!". The answer shows the voice got there, not that the other person understood every word.
3.scenario: An airman wants to know whether IP gets through to a server on another network. The airman pings the server's IP address: an ICMP echo request goes out, and the server answers with an ICMP echo reply. The reply shows Network Layer to Network Layer reachability; it says nothing about the server's applications.
3.example: Tapping a microphone and hearing the thump from the speakers shows the sound path works, but not that the speech will be clear. In the course: Ping sends an ICMP echo request to a destination IP address, Block Text p.33.

3.summary: Routing protocols are Network Layer protocols responsible for path determination and packet switching; routers use them to learn from other routers about available networks and to build and maintain routing tables.
3.deeper: Routing protocols implement routing algorithms to build and maintain routing tables, and they apply metric costs to the available paths to determine the best path to the destination network. A routing protocol exchanges information packets with other internetwork routers, so routers learn paths from periodic updates about known networks. Examples are RIP, IGRP, OSPF, EIGRP and BGP. Compare routed protocols, commonly called network protocols: they provide the logical addressing a router uses to decide where to send a packet, as IP does in the Internet protocol suite, and they are transported, or routed, over an internetwork by routing protocols. One simplified way to look at it: routed protocols are messages, and routing protocols deliver those messages. Interior gateway protocols route within an autonomous system; exterior gateway protocols route between them.
3.analogy: Routed protocols are the letters; routing protocols are the postal workers who compare notes on which roads are open and carry each letter on.
3.scenario: Two routers at an airman's base run OSPF. They exchange information about the networks each one knows and build their routing tables. When a workstation sends an IP packet across the base, the routers use those tables to carry it to the right network.
3.example: Delivery drivers share news about closed roads so each can plan the best way to deliver the parcels. In the course: Routing protocols are Network Layer protocols that are responsible for path determination and packet (traffic) switching, Block Text p.33.

3.summary: Static routes are router table entries established by the network administrator; they do not change until the administrator changes them, so information takes the same route every time.
3.deeper: Static routes are simple to configure and work well where network traffic is relatively predictable and network design is relatively simple; they are also useful for controlling security and reducing traffic. Because static routing cannot react to network changes, it is generally considered unsuitable for today's large, diverse networks. Routers already know the networks directly connected to them if their interfaces are functional, so static routes are configured for paths that are not directly connected; they are added to the routing table as reachable network destinations. A default route is a special static route, the gateway of last resort, used when no route to the destination is known. Dynamic routes are the other way to learn paths: routers learn them from other routers through routing protocols, adjust to changing network circumstances, and recalculate routes automatically at regular intervals.
3.analogy: A static route is like a printed bus timetable on a wall: it is easy to read and right for a quiet line, but it does not change when a road closes until someone prints a new one.
3.scenario: An airman's small site has one path to headquarters and very predictable traffic. The airman enters a static route for that path. Months later the link fails; the static route does not react, and traffic keeps heading the same way until the airman changes the entry.
3.example: A note on the fridge that always says "take Main Street to school" gives the same route every day, even on the day Main Street is closed. In the course: Static routes are established by the network administrator and do not change until the network administrator changes them, Block Text p.33.
