3.summary: A default route, often called the gateway of last resort, is a special static route the system administrator defines as the path to take when no route to the destination is known.
3.deeper: Routers learn paths from static routes, default routes or dynamic routes. A default route is a type of static route, manually defined by the system administrator. It is the route to which all non-routable packets are sent, and it can be designated as a routing table entry for all packets destined to networks unknown to the router. This ensures that all messages have an outbound path from the router to some other router that may have more detailed routing entries able to route the packet. Without one, a packet that arrives for a network with no listing in the routing table is discarded; the default route stops the router from discarding messages that may be valid. A default route lives in a router; a default gateway is the setting on a host.
3.analogy: A default route is like a post office's rule for unknown addresses: anything it cannot sort itself goes on to the regional centre, which has a fuller directory.
3.scenario: A packet reaches an airman's router for a network that is not in its routing table. Because the administrator defined a default route, the router does not discard it: it sends it out the gateway of last resort to the next router, which may have more detailed routing entries.

3.summary: A routing table holds the best path to known destination networks; a router matches each packet's destination address with an entry in it to find the next hop.
3.deeper: A router fills its routing table in two ways. First, it uses the IP addresses and subnet masks configured on its interfaces to extract each subnet address and place it in the table. Second, it learns about distant subnets from other routers, and those learned networks are placed in the table too. Paths can be learned from static routes, default routes or dynamic routes. When a router knows about the same destination from more than one routing source, it chooses the path with the lowest Administrative Distance (AD): the lower the AD, the more trustworthy the route, so a path learned from EIGRP (AD 90) is used before one learned from OSPF (AD 110). An IP routing table consists of destination address and next hop pairs, read like this: to get to network 172.16.3.0, send the packet out Fast Ethernet interface 0/0 (Fa0/0). Routing algorithms place the lowest cost path in the table. The routers do not monitor whether packets reach their destination; error reporting is left to ICMP. Whatever the method, the overall goal of a router is to build a routing table.
3.analogy: A routing table is like the signboard at a road junction: for each town it shows only one arrow, the best road out of this junction.
3.scenario: A router learns a path to the same remote network from both EIGRP and OSPF. It trusts the source with the lower Administrative Distance, so the EIGRP path goes into the routing table. A packet for that network is then sent out the interface the entry names.
3.example: A phone's contact list keeps one best number for each friend, and a call uses whatever number is listed. In the course: Routing tables contain the best path to known destination networks used by routers to route packets, Block Text p.36.

3.summary: Routing metrics are the values routing algorithms use to determine the best route, such as path length, hop count, reliability, delay, bandwidth, load and communication cost.
3.deeper:
Routing tables hold the best path to known destination networks, and routing algorithms use many different metrics to decide that one route is better than another. Sophisticated algorithms can combine several metrics into a single (hybrid) metric. Path length is the most common metric: where administrators assign arbitrary costs to each link, path length is the sum of the costs of each link traversed. Reliability is the dependability of each link, usually its bit-error rate. Delay is the time required to move a packet from source to destination; it depends on the bandwidth of intermediate links, port queues at each router, congestion and physical distance, which makes it a common and useful metric. Bandwidth is the available traffic capacity of a link, but a route through a faster link is not always better: if that link is busier, the packet may take longer. Communication cost, set by the network administrator, matters to organizations that care more about operating expenses than performance.

Hop count: some routing protocols define hop count as the number of passes (hops) through internetworking devices, such as routers, that a packet must take from source to destination. RIP's metric is hop count.

Load: the degree to which a network resource, such as a router, is busy. It can be calculated in several ways, including CPU utilization and packets processed per second; monitoring these all the time can itself be resource intensive.
3.analogy: Choosing a route by metrics is like choosing a road home: the number of junctions, how often the road is closed, the travel time, the number of lanes, how jammed it is right now and the tolls all count.
3.scenario: An airman compares two routes. One passes fewer routers, but its router is very busy; the other has more hops through quiet routers with fast links. Depending on whether the algorithm weighs hop count, load or delay, either route could come out best.
3.example: A taxi driver picks a route by distance, traffic and tolls, not just by the shortest line on the map. In the course: Routing algorithms use many different metrics to determine the best route, Block Text p.36.

3.summary: Routing algorithms initialize and maintain routing tables: an algorithm takes weighted metric costs to calculate overall optimal path costs to destination networks, and the lowest cost path is placed in the routing table.
3.deeper: A router uses a mathematical formula, an algorithm, to assess the metric costs associated with networks. The route information in a routing table can vary depending on the routing algorithm used. When a router receives an incoming packet, it checks the destination network address and tries to associate it with a next hop from the routing table. Routing algorithms can be differentiated by several characteristics: the goals of the algorithm design affect how the resulting routing protocol operates, and each algorithm has a different impact on network and router resources. The two primary types are distance vector and link state. Dynamic routing algorithms use a variety of metrics, and sophisticated ones can base route selection on multiple metrics, combined in a single (hybrid) metric.
3.analogy: A routing algorithm is like a judge at a contest who scores each entry on several weighted points, adds them up, and posts only the winner on the board.

3.summary: Distance vector algorithms determine the direction (vector) and distance to any link in the internetwork, building their routing tables from their neighbors' routing tables.
3.deeper: Distance vector algorithms gather information on destination networks through broadcast routing update messages, sent when the network topology changes and at regular intervals. When a router receives a routing update that changes an entry, it updates its routing table and immediately begins transmitting routing updates to inform its neighbor routers, independently of the regularly scheduled updates. This is often called "routing by rumor", since the routers don't know where the information initially came from and must assume it is correct. Advantages: they are simple to understand and configure, do not require much from the router's processor to maintain the routing table, and are less expensive to implement and support. Disadvantages: they are limited by hop count, making them unsuitable for large networks; variable length subnet masking is not supported in RIPv1; and because they update by broadcast and build their routing tables from their neighbor's routing tables, they route on information that cannot be verified as accurate. Distance vector algorithms send larger updates, but only to their neighboring routers. RIP is a distance vector protocol.
3.analogy: Distance vector routing is like asking a neighbour for directions: they say "that way, about five streets", and you trust them without seeing the map yourself.
3.scenario: A router running a distance vector protocol learns of a changed route from its neighbor. It updates its routing table and immediately tells its own neighbors, without knowing where the information first came from. Its table holds a direction and a distance for each destination, built from what its neighbors reported.

3.summary: Link state algorithms, also known as shortest path first (SPF) algorithms, build a complete topological map of the entire area in memory, so each router sees the entire path to the destination network.
3.deeper: Because a link state router sees the entire path, it can make sure the path is valid and is the best path available. Link state algorithms use multicast link state advertisements to tell the other routers in the area the status of their connected links; a router that receives one copies the information for its own use and immediately resends it through its other interfaces, which gives very fast convergence. Only the directly affected routers generate the message, and every receiving router is assured that the information is valid. Link state algorithms support variable length subnet masks (VLSM), and each router sends information describing the state of its own links. Basically, link state algorithms send small updates everywhere, while distance vector algorithms send larger updates only to their neighboring routers. Because they converge more quickly, link state algorithms are less prone to routing loops; on the other hand, they need more CPU power and memory than distance vector algorithms, so they can be more expensive to implement and support. Both types perform well in most circumstances. OSPF is a link state protocol.
3.analogy: A link state router is like a driver with a complete road map of the region: the whole route can be checked before setting out. A distance vector router is more like a driver who asks for directions at each junction and trusts what is said.
3.scenario: An airman compares the two algorithm types for a large network. Every router keeps a full map of the area and small updates go everywhere; link state converges more quickly, so it is less prone to routing loops. The trade-off is that each router needs more CPU power and memory.
3.example: A hiker who carries a map of the whole park can see every trail to the lake before choosing one. In the course: Link state algorithms build a complete topological map of the entire area in memory, Block Text p.38.

3.summary: Convergence of new routing information takes longer with RIP, whose updates pass one router at a time, and is very fast with link state routers, which resend each advertisement at once.
3.deeper: RIP sends its updates only to a router's directly connected neighbors, and the network is updated one router at a time, resulting in longer convergence times: the broadcast cannot travel beyond the directly connected neighbor routers, because the first router interface it encounters stops it. Link state routers do it differently. When they receive a multicast link state advertisement, they copy the information for their own use and immediately resend the message through their other interfaces, which allows very fast convergence of new information. Because they converge more quickly, link state algorithms are less prone to routing loops than distance vector algorithms. In OSPF, the Shortest Path First algorithm allows fast convergence; EIGRP has fast convergence when a feasible successor is available; and a balanced hybrid aims to ensure fast convergence to network changes.
3.analogy: Slow convergence is like news passed by word of mouth from one neighbor to the next; fast convergence is like each person who hears it phoning everyone they know at once.
3.scenario: A link goes down at the edge of an airman's network. With RIP, the change reaches the far routers only after each router in turn has updated and passed it on. With a link state protocol, each router that receives the advertisement resends it at once, so all routers learn of the change quickly.
3.example: A rumour that passes one person at a time reaches the whole town slowly, while a town-wide announcement reaches everyone at once. 3.summary: An IP network assigned more than one subnet mask has Variable Length Subnet Masks (VLSM); RIP does not support VLSM because its routing updates carry no subnet mask information, while RIPv2, OSPF and EIGRP include it.
3.deeper:
RIP does not support variable length subnet masking, because it does not include subnet mask information in its routing updates; this is listed among the disadvantages of distance vector algorithms (VLSM is not supported in RIPv1). RIPv2 improves on RIP by allowing VLSM, as it includes subnet mask data in all routing updates. Support for VLSM is one of the benefits of link state algorithms. EIGRP supports VLSM too, because subnet mask information is exchanged in its updates.

3.summary: A balanced hybrid routing protocol combines the advantages of the two primary types, distance vector and link state; EIGRP is the example.
3.deeper: The two primary classes of routing protocols each have their drawbacks. Distance vector protocols are not well suited for large networks and use too much of the network bandwidth; link state protocols were too complicated and often required additional investments in equipment and expensive additional training for network managers. A hybrid that takes the advantages of each would be simple to configure and comprehend, would not use excessive amounts of bandwidth, would ensure fast convergence to network changes and would not require additional training for the management staff. Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP) is known as a "balanced hybrid" for this reason. It resembles distance vector because it uses distance vectors and maintains copies of its neighbor's routing tables, and it resembles link state because topology changes trigger updates by multicast.
3.analogy: A balanced hybrid is like a car that takes the simple controls of one model and the quick response of another, leaving behind the drawbacks of each.
3.scenario: An airman compares routing options for a growing network. Distance vector would be simple but uses too much bandwidth in a large network; link state converges fast but is complicated and costly to support. EIGRP, a balanced hybrid, combines the advantages of the two.

3.summary: RIP uses a distance vector algorithm; its metric is hop count, limited to 15, and it sends broadcast routing updates every 30 seconds and when the network topology changes.
3.deeper: RIP is an interior gateway protocol. RIP routers keep only the best route (the one with the lowest metric value) to a destination. After updating its routing table, a router immediately begins sending routing updates to inform other routers of the change, independently of the regularly scheduled updates. These updates go only to a router's directly connected neighbors and are passed on one router at a time, which results in longer convergence times: the broadcast message cannot travel beyond the directly connected neighbors, because the first router interface it meets stops it. Another drawback is that RIP does not support variable length subnet masking, because its routing updates carry no subnet mask information. RIPv2 improves on RIP by including subnet mask data in all routing updates, and RIPng was developed for IPv6. OSPF was later created as a solution to RIP's inability to handle routing in large, diverse networks.
3.analogy: RIP is like news passed along a line of people by word of mouth: each person tells only the next, so the news reaches the end of the line slowly.
3.scenario: A link in an airman's RIP network goes down. The router next to it updates its routing table and broadcasts the change to its directly connected neighbors. They update and pass it on, one router at a time, so routers far away learn of the change last.

3.summary: In OSPF, cost is the metric based on a reference bandwidth divided by the interface bandwidth; the costs of the interfaces along a path add up to the total cost to the destination.
3.deeper: OSPF's metric is cost, based by default on a 100 Mbps reference bandwidth divided by the interface bandwidth; the administrator can adjust it. The cost of each interface is added up to determine the total cost to the destination. Links of gigabit and higher data rates may create issues in today's networks, so the bandwidth reference is changed to avoid having faster links appear as the same cost as slower links. More generally, path length is the most common routing metric: some routing protocols let network administrators assign arbitrary costs to each network link, and path length is then the sum of the costs associated with each link traversed. Routing algorithms take weighted metric costs to calculate overall path costs, and the lowest cost path is placed in the routing table.
3.analogy: Cost is like a toll on each stretch of road: add up the tolls along a route and take the route with the smallest total.
3.scenario: An OSPF router has two paths to a destination network. It takes the cost of each interface along the first path and adds them up, then does the same for the second path. The path with the lower total cost goes into its routing table.

3.summary: OSPF is a link state routing protocol that sends information describing the state of its own links to all the routers within the same hierarchical area; its metric is cost based on bandwidth.
3.deeper: OSPF was created in the late 1980s as a solution to RIP's inability to handle routing in large, diverse networks. Interface information, the metrics used and other variables are included in OSPF's Link State Advertisements (LSAs), and OSPF routers use Dijkstra's Shortest Path First (SPF) algorithm to calculate the shortest path to each router. Its metric is cost, based on a 100 Mbps reference bandwidth divided by the interface bandwidth; the cost of each interface is added up to give the total cost to the destination. OSPF builds in memory a shortest path tree for every network it knows and maintains an awareness of the state of all routers and routes within the network. It operates best within a hierarchy: an autonomous system is divided into areas, area border routers join them, and Area 0, the backbone, connects to all other areas. IP subnet masks are included with each advertised destination, which enables variable-length subnet masks: classless routing. OSPF keeps a neighbor table, a topology table and a routing table. Advantages: hierarchical routing supports very large networks, fast convergence, classless routing, and smaller updates sent only when the topology changes. Disadvantages: a complex structured topology, highly trained staff, considerable memory, and more processing power as the topology database grows. OSPFv3 supports IPv6.
3.analogy: OSPF is like a large company split into departments: each department keeps its own detailed map, and a central office joins the departments together. Running it well takes a trained staff and a lot of filing space.
3.scenario: An airman's network has outgrown RIP. The airman moves it to OSPF, divides the autonomous system into areas joined to Area 0, and expects fast convergence and small updates only on topology changes. The cost is routers with considerable memory and staff trained to configure a large OSPF network.

3.summary: The OSPF backbone, commonly Area 0, is the mandatory area connected to all other areas; it distributes routing information between them.
3.deeper: OSPF operates best within a hierarchy: the autonomous system is divided into areas, as a single area or as multiple areas. In a multi-area design, Area 0, the backbone, is mandatory and is connected to all other areas. It consists of all area border routers, networks not wholly contained in any area and their attached routers. The backbone is itself an OSPF area, and its routers use the same procedures and algorithms as other area routers. The backbone topology is invisible to all intra-area routers, as the individual area topologies are to the backbone. Each area should be a contiguous address space separate from other areas: overlapping addresses defeat the advantage of summarizing each area connected to the backbone, and losing that summarizing causes larger routing tables in both the area routers and the backbone routers.
3.analogy: The backbone is like the head office of a company with regional branches: every branch is linked to it, and it passes each branch's news on to the others.
3.scenario: An airman plans a multi-area OSPF network for a base. Area 1, Area 2 and Area 3 each hold contiguous networks. Area 0 must exist and connect to all three, because the backbone distributes routing information between the areas.

3.summary: A topology table is a router's overall picture of its routes: in OSPF it holds the LSAs received from all routers in the same area; in EIGRP it holds all destinations advertised by neighboring routers.
3.deeper: In OSPF, the topology table is an overall picture of the active router interfaces participating in OSPF. It contains the collection of LSAs received from all routers in the same area; because those routers share the same information, they have identical topology tables. An area's topology is invisible to routers outside the area, so OSPF passes less routing traffic than it would if the AS were not partitioned. The SPF algorithm uses the topology table to calculate entries for the routing table: each router calculates a shortest-path tree with itself as the root. In EIGRP, the topology table contains all destinations advertised by neighboring routers. Each entry holds the destination address and a list of the neighbors that advertised it, with the advertised metric for each. Each enabled protocol fills its own table, and DUAL FSM acts on it to find the best route (successor) and a backup route (feasible successor); the successors are extracted from it to build the routing table.
3.analogy: A topology table is like a team's shared whiteboard of every road report: the routing table is the short list of best roads written up from it.
3.scenario: An airman checks two routers in the same OSPF area and finds their topology tables identical, since both hold the LSAs of every router in the area. On an EIGRP router, the topology table instead lists each destination with the neighbors that advertised it, and DUAL FSM picks the successor from it.
3.example: A newsroom keeps every reporter's notes on one board, and the editor picks the best stories from it for the front page. In the course: The topology table contains the collection of LSAs received from all routers in the same area, Block Text p.41.

3.summary: Dijkstra's Shortest Path First (SPF) is the algorithm OSPF routers use on the topology table to calculate a shortest-path tree, with each router as the root of its own tree.
3.deeper: Link state algorithms are also known as shortest path first algorithms. OSPF routers use Dijkstra's Shortest Path First (SPF) algorithm to calculate the shortest path to each router, and the SPF algorithm is the basis for OSPF operations. The topology table holds the collection of LSAs received from all routers in the same area. The algorithm uses the information from the topology table to calculate entries for insertion into the routing table: each router calculates a shortest-path tree, with itself as the root, for each known sub-network, and the tree in turn yields entries into the routing table. OSPF builds this shortest path tree in memory for every network it knows. The SPF algorithm allows fast convergence, but it uses more processing power as the size of the topology database increases.
3.analogy: SPF is like a person drawing a family tree with themselves at the top: everyone else appears by the shortest line of connection to them, and each person who draws one puts themselves at the top of their own tree.
3.scenario: An OSPF router has collected the LSAs of every router in its area in its topology table. It runs the SPF algorithm on that table, builds a shortest-path tree with itself as the root, and takes the routing table entries from the tree.
3.example: A delivery driver plans routes from the depot outward, keeping only the shortest way to each stop. In the course: from the topology table generated from LSAs, each router calculates a shortest-path tree, with itself as the root for each known sub-network, Block Text p.42.

3.summary: Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP) is a balanced hybrid interior routing protocol that keeps a neighbor table, a topology table and a routing table, with a best route and a backup route to each destination.
3.deeper:
EIGRP is often called a balanced hybrid because it combines the advantages of link state protocols with those of distance vector protocols; its metrics are bandwidth and delay by default. Propagation of its updates is automatically bounded so that only the routers that need the information are updated. Its algorithm is the Diffusing Update Algorithm (DUAL) Finite State Machine (FSM). An EIGRP router keeps a separate neighbor table, topology table and routing table for each protocol supported. The neighbor table records each new neighbor's address and interface; a neighbor's hello packet advertises a hold time, and if no hello arrives within it, DUAL FSM is informed of the topology change. The topology table contains all destinations advertised by neighboring routers, each with the neighbors that advertised it and their advertised metric. Advantages: fast convergence when a feasible successor is available, support for variable length subnet masks, smaller updates sent only on a topology change, and scaling to large networks. Disadvantages: higher memory requirements for its tables, a complex routing algorithm that can be CPU-intensive during network instability, and no area concept.

Successor: DUAL FSM acts on the topology table to determine the best route, the successor, and the backup route, the feasible successor. The successors to each known network are extracted from the topology table to build the routing table. If a successor route fails, the feasible successor is placed in the routing table.
3.analogy: EIGRP is like a driver who keeps a contact list, a map of every road the contacts mention, and a chosen route with a planned detour: if the chosen road closes, the detour is ready at once.
3.scenario: An airman's EIGRP router hears from a new neighbor and records it in the neighbor table. The destinations its neighbors advertise fill the topology table, and DUAL FSM picks a successor and a feasible successor for each. When the successor route fails, the router places the feasible successor in its routing table right away.
3.example: A traveller who books a main flight and also notes a backup flight can switch at once if the first is cancelled. In the course: the topology table is acted on by the DUAL FSM to determine the best route (successor) and backup route (feasible successor), Block Text p.43.

3.summary: Exterior gateway protocols (EGPs) route information between autonomous systems, such as from one Air Force base to another; BGP is the predominant one.
3.deeper: Interior gateway protocols such as RIP, OSPF and EIGRP route information within an autonomous system. When communications are required between autonomous systems, a different type of routing protocol is used: an exterior gateway protocol. Exterior gateway routers move information between autonomous systems. Routing from one Air Force base to another is an example of routing between autonomous systems, and Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) is an example of an exterior gateway protocol. The Internet is composed of autonomous systems that use BGP-4 to implement inter-AS routing policies; BGP is the predominant EGP in use today and the protocol that runs the Internet. Exterior routing algorithms are more complex than interior routing algorithms because they must learn and track a greater number of routers and routes.
3.analogy: Interior and exterior gateway protocols are like a city's local streets and the highways between cities: local streets move traffic around one town, and highways connect towns to each other.
3.scenario: An airman's base routes its own networks with OSPF. Traffic to another base leaves its autonomous system, so the routing between the two bases uses an exterior gateway protocol, BGP.
3.example: A company's internal mail room handles letters between its own offices, while letters to other companies go through the national postal service. In the course: EGPs are used to route information between autonomous systems, Block Text p.44.

3.summary: Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) is the exterior gateway protocol that exchanges routing information between autonomous systems while guaranteeing loop-free path selection; it runs the Internet.
3.deeper:
The Internet is composed of autonomous systems that use BGP-4 to implement inter-AS routing policies, and BGP is the protocol used between Internet service providers (ISPs). It is the predominant exterior gateway protocol in use today. BGP supports reliable updates by using TCP for acknowledgements of its update messages, and it uses periodic keep-alives to maintain TCP connectivity. Unlike interior gateway protocols, it has no mechanism for automatic neighbor discovery: the network administrator must manually define BGP neighbors and initiate a TCP connection-oriented session between them. BGP is capable of detecting routing loops.

Path Vector: BGP is considered a path vector protocol. Small, standardized networks can use a single metric to describe the best path (RIP uses hop count), but no single metric can describe the best path across autonomous systems running multiple IGPs on diverse media. Instead, BGP uses many route parameters, called attributes or path vectors, that describe each path and define routing policies; its route selection algorithm uses the attribute list to select a single best path to each known destination.
3.analogy: BGP is like two embassies that agree in writing who their contacts are, confirm every message they receive, and compare several qualities of each travel route rather than its length alone.
3.scenario: An airman's base must exchange routes with another autonomous system. The network administrator defines the BGP neighbor by hand and starts a TCP session with it. Each update is acknowledged through TCP, and BGP weighs the attributes of each path to pick a single best path to each destination.
3.example: Two shipping companies trading cargo routes confirm each message they receive and compare several facts about each route before choosing one. In the course: the primary function of BGP is to exchange routing information between autonomous systems while guaranteeing loop-free path selection, Block Text p.44.

3.summary: A Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG) is a methodology for standardized secure installation and maintenance of computer software and hardware.
3.deeper:
STIGs, when implemented, lock down common and typically permissive software to further reduce vulnerabilities. The term was coined in 1998 by the Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA), which creates configuration documents in support of the Department of Defense (DoD). The guidelines include recommended administrative processes and span the devices' lifecycle, and STIG scanning software is used to implement and validate proper configuration. A STIG helps in configuring a desktop computer or network device, since most operating systems are not inherently secure: it describes how to minimize network-based attacks and prevent system access, whether the attacker is physically at the machine or comes over a network. STIGs also describe maintenance processes such as software updates and vulnerability patching, and advanced STIGs might cover the design of a network, with the configuration of routers, firewalls, domain name servers and switches. The STIGs and the NSA Guides are the configuration standards for DoD Information Assurance (IA) and IA-enabled devices and systems.

Logical security: for routing devices, logical security comes in the form of Access Control Lists (ACLs) and STIGs.
3.analogy: A STIG is like a checklist for closing up a building for the night: every door and window on the list is locked the same way each time, and the list also says when to check the locks again.
3.scenario: An airman sets up a new router. Following the router STIG, the airman locks down settings that are permissive out of the box, so the router is hard to reach without authorization, whether at the machine or over the network. Later, the same STIG guides software updates and vulnerability patching, and scanning software checks the configuration.
3.example: A recipe card makes every cook prepare a dish the same safe way, every time. In the course: A Security Technical Implementation Guide or STIG is a methodology for standardized secure installation and maintenance of computer software and hardware, Block Text p.46.

4.summary: The core layer is the top of Cisco's hierarchical model, often called a high-speed backbone; its only purpose is to transport large amounts of traffic reliably and quickly.
4.deeper:
The core layer is literally the core of the network. At the top of the hierarchy, its only purpose is to transport large amounts of traffic reliably and quickly, and the traffic it transports is common to most users. User data is processed at the distribution layer, which forwards requests to the core when necessary. Core devices are normally high-speed switches and routers.

A failure in the core, either by a faulty link or a faulty device, may affect every user, especially to the outside world, so fault tolerance through redundancy is essential. Since the core transports large volumes of traffic, speed and latency are major concerns.

Design considerations: Workgroups: don't support workgroup access by connecting devices that belong to the access layer; this defeats the concept of the hierarchical model. Scalability: avoid expanding the core when the internetwork grows (adding routers); if performance becomes an issue, give preference to upgrades over expansion. Reliability and Redundancy: design for high reliability and redundancy, with Data Link technologies and media such as fiber optics via FDDI, FastEthernet with redundant links, or ATM. Protocols: select routing protocols with lower convergence times or extremely fast and efficient layer 2 switching devices, and do not burden core devices with processes such as access-list checking, data encryption or address translation.
4.analogy: The core layer is like an interstate highway between cities: it carries heavy traffic quickly, it has no driveways for single houses, and when it gets crowded it is widened rather than given more exits.
4.scenario: Users at a base complain that traffic is slow when it crosses the core. The airman's plan upgrades the two core routers instead of adding a third, keeps the redundant links between them, and leaves access-list checking and address translation to the distribution layer so the core can keep switching packets at top speed.
4.example: A main water line carries water for a whole town; if it breaks, every house is affected, so it is built with spare capacity. The core layer carries traffic for most users the same way. In the course: The core layer's only purpose is to transport large amounts of traffic reliably and quickly, Block Text p.50.

4.summary: The distribution layer is the communication point between the access layer and the core layer; it provides routing, filtering and WAN access and is the place to implement network policies.
4.deeper:
The primary function of the distribution layer is to provide routing, filtering, WAN access and to determine how packets can access the core when necessary. It must determine the fastest way that user requests are serviced, for example how a file request is forwarded to a server. All traffic for remote services is handled by the distribution layer. After it determines the best path, it forwards the request to the core layer. User data is processed at the distribution layer.

The distribution layer is the place to implement policies for the network: tools such as access lists, packet filtering, queuing, security and network policies, including address translation and firewalls; redistribution between routing protocols, including static routing; routing between VLANs and other workgroup support functions; and defining broadcast and multicast domains. Things to avoid here are functions that exclusively belong to one of the other layers, such as end-user devices.

The distribution layer switch is the aggregation point for multiple access switches and must be capable of handling a large amount of traffic. Both layer 2 and layer 3 network devices are employed here; the size and needs of the network decide which devices are appropriate.
4.analogy: The distribution layer is like a dispatcher at a depot: requests come in from the local offices, the dispatcher applies the rules and picks the fastest route, then hands each load to the long-haul trucks.
4.scenario: A user asks for a file on a server at another site. The request leaves the user's access switch and reaches the distribution layer. There the request is checked against the access lists, the fastest path to the server is determined, and the request is forwarded to the core layer for transport.
4.example: A sorting center decides which truck each package goes on and checks the shipping rules before passing it to the highway carrier. The distribution layer does the same for user requests. In the course: The distribution layer is the communication point between the access layer and the core layer, Block Text p.51.

4.summary: The access layer is the tier of Cisco's hierarchical model that ensures frames are delivered to the end user computers; it is sometimes called the desktop layer.
4.deeper:
Cisco's hierarchical internetworking model divides a network into three layers: core, distribution and access. The access layer ensures that frames are delivered to the end user computers. It is sometimes referred to as the desktop layer because the majority of devices connected to the access switches are desktop computers.

The network resources that most users need, such as printers and certain servers, are available locally. The switches deployed at this layer must be able to handle connecting multiple desktop devices to the distribution layer. They are characterized as having many ports and low cost. The functions included at this layer are shared bandwidth devices, switched bandwidth devices, Layer 2 functions such as VLAN membership, and traffic filtering based on MAC.

Workgroups connect here, not at the core: connecting devices that belong to the access layer to the core defeats the concept of the hierarchical model.
4.analogy: The access layer is like the front desk of each office in a large building: every worker deals with the front desk of their own office, and the front desk passes things up to the rest of the building.
4.scenario: An airman sets up the desktop computers of a new office. They plug into an access switch, a low-cost switch with many ports, which connects them to the distribution layer. The switch also handles VLAN membership for each port and can filter traffic based on MAC. Frames meant for those desktops are delivered to them at the access layer.
4.example: A mail carrier takes the letters from the local post office and brings each one to the right house on the route. The access layer does that last stretch for frames. In the course: The access layer ensures that frames are delivered to the end user computers, Block Text p.52.

5.summary: A subnet is a logical division of a network of connected devices based on the IP address: a network within a network.
5.deeper:
Users need to talk to printers and email programs need to talk to servers, so each of these needs an IP address. It is often necessary to group things on a network together, for both organizational and efficiency's sake. For example, a company may want each user to see only the printers of their own department, the marketing department or the sales offices. Organizing the IP addresses of those printers into unique subnets does this.

A subnet is a logical division of a network of connected devices based on the IP address. It is a separate and identifiable portion of an organization's network, typically arranged on one floor, building or geographical location: a network within a network. Subnetting rules apply only to Class A, B and C addresses; Class D and Class E addresses do not possess subnet masks and cannot be subnetted.

Host: each device on a subnet has an IP address that logically associates it with the others on the same subnet, and in terms of IP addressing and subnets these devices are referred to as hosts. In the example there is a network (the company), divided into logical subnets (marketing and sales), each with its own hosts (users and printers). Addressing by subnet also keeps devices on one subnet from getting confused with hosts on the other subnet.
5.analogy: A subnet is like a department inside a company: the company is one organization, but each department has its own staff and its own printers, and people find their own department first.
5.scenario: An airman's unit wants each user to see only the printers of their own department. The marketing users and printers are organized into one subnet and the sales users and printers into another. Each computer and printer is a host with an IP address that associates it with the others on its subnet.
5.example: An apartment building has one street address, and each floor holds its own group of apartments. A subnet is one such group inside a larger network. In the course: A subnet is a logical division of a network of connected network devices based on the IP address, Block Text p.53.

5.summary: Subnetting divides a network into smaller portions called subnets by borrowing bits from the host portion of the IP address.
5.deeper:
To subnet a network is to create logical divisions of it. Subnetting involves dividing the network into smaller portions called subnets, and it is done by borrowing bits from the host portion of the IP address: the networking portion borrows bits from the host portion. The IP address then has three components: the network part, the subnet part and the host part.

A Class C address normally has 24 bits for the network address and eight for the host. Borrowing the left-most host bit to identify the subnet gives two subnets: if the bit is a 0 that is one subnet, if it is a 1 that is the second. With only one borrowed bit there can only be two possible subnets. How many bits should be borrowed is the same question as how many subnets the network should have, and the subnet mask indicates it. More bits borrowed means fewer individually addressable hosts on the network.

These rules apply only to Class A, B and C addresses; Class D and Class E addresses do not possess subnet masks and cannot be subnetted. Class A provides the most available subnets because it has more host bits to borrow from, and the host requirement is taken into account when subnetting. Designing a simple network is based on two things: how many subnets are needed and/or how many hosts are needed for each subnet. Benefits of subnetting: reduced network traffic, optimized performance and simplified management.
5.analogy: Subnetting is like dividing a large office floor with partitions: each partition you add makes another room, and every new room leaves less space for desks in each one.
5.scenario: An airman must split a network for two departments. One bit is borrowed from the host portion: hosts with a 0 in that bit are on one subnet and hosts with a 1 on the other. If more departments needed their own subnets, more bits would be borrowed, leaving fewer hosts on each subnet.
5.example: Cutting a pizza into more slices gives more pieces, but each slice is smaller. Subnetting trades host addresses for subnets the same way. In the course: Subnetting involves dividing the network into smaller portions called subnets, Block Text p.54.

5.summary: A subnet mask is a 32-bit number that divides an IP address into a network address and a host address; it indicates how many bits are borrowed from the host component.
5.deeper:
Subnetting borrows bits from the host portion of an IP address, so the address then has three components: the network part, the subnet part and the host part. The subnet mask tells how many bits are borrowed, or in other words how many subnets the network has.

A subnet mask is a 32-bit number used to differentiate the network component of an IP address by dividing the IP address into a network address and a host address. All that a subnet mask does is indicate how many bits are being "borrowed" from the host component; this is the foundation of all subnetting. The mask has its name because it literally masks out the host bits being borrowed from the host address portion. The number 255 represents the network number in the subnet mask. For example, the mask 255.255.255.128 on a Class C address indicates which bits of the host part will be used to determine the subnet number.

The three parts of an IP address work in tandem and act as one: they are different pieces of the same puzzle.
5.analogy: A subnet mask is like a stencil laid over a long number: the stencil shows which digits belong to the street, which to the block and which to the house, without changing the number underneath.
5.scenario: An airman looks at a Class C address with the mask 255.255.255.128. The three 255s stand for the network number. The last part of the mask shows that one bit is borrowed from the host portion to identify the subnet, so the mask divides the address into its network and host parts.
5.example: A ruler laid over a page marks where one section ends and the next begins, without changing the page. A subnet mask marks where the network part ends in an IP address. 5.summary: Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR), pronounced "cider", is used to represent IP addresses: the address, a slash, then the number of bits used in the mask.
5.deeper:
IP address classes are not used anymore other than to understand the basic concepts of IP addressing. Instead, Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) is used to represent IP addresses. An address and its mask can be written as two separate values (an address and a mask), or in CIDR as one value: the network address with the number of mask bits tacked on after a slash, such as 205.112.45.60/25.

The idea behind CIDR is to adapt the concept of subnetting to the entire Internet. Classless addressing means that instead of breaking a particular network into subnets, networks can be aggregated into larger supernets.

Why use CIDR? It is a much more efficient allocator of the IP address space: a network admin can carve out a number of host addresses that is closer to what is required than with the class approach.
5.analogy: CIDR is like a shoe size written with its width, such as "9/W": one short label carries both the size and the detail needed to use it, so no second card is needed.
5.scenario: An airman reads a network record that lists 205.112.45.60/25. The part before the slash is the network address; the /25 after it is the number of bits used in the mask. The same record could have listed the address and the mask as two separate values.
5.example: A street address with an apartment number, such as "12 Main St / Apt 4", puts two pieces of information in one short line. CIDR writes an address and its mask together in the same way. In the course: Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) is used to represent IP addresses, Block Text p.58.

5.summary: An IP network assigned more than one subnet mask is said to have a Variable Length Subnet Mask (VLSM), so each subnet can have a different number of hosts.
5.deeper:
When an IP network is assigned more than one subnet mask, it is said to have a Variable Length Subnet Mask (VLSM). VLSM is what is used when subnetting a subnet, based on network needs: any one subnet can be broken down into further subnets by indicating the proper VLSM. This makes IP addressing more efficient by allowing each subnet to have a different number of hosts, depending on their requirements, which reduces the number of wasted addresses.

RIP 1 routers matter here. Originally, the IP addressing scheme and the RIP 1 routing protocol did not take into consideration different subnet masks on the same network. A RIP 1 router just has an address to work with, with no knowledge of how many bits are used for the network address and how many for the host address, so it makes assumptions: if it has a subnet of the same network number on its local interface, it assumes the same mask as that interface; otherwise it applies a classful mask. RIP1 only allows a single subnet mask, making it impossible to get the full benefit of VLSM.

A newer routing protocol such as Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) or RIP2 sends the network prefix length or mask value along with route advertisements from router to router. With these in use, VLSM can be used to its full potential, with more than one subnet or sub-subnets.
5.analogy: VLSM is like cutting rooms of different sizes from one floor plan: a big room where many people work and a small one for two, instead of identical rooms that leave empty desks.
5.scenario: A network has one subnet with many hosts and another with only a few. Giving each subnet the mask that fits its needs wastes fewer addresses. The routers run RIP 1, which only allows a single mask, so the airman plans to move to OSPF or RIP2, which send the mask with their route advertisements.
5.example: A clothing shop stocks shirts in several sizes so each customer gets one that fits instead of one size for all. VLSM gives each subnet a size that fits. 6.summary: Physical topology refers to the physical interconnection of network devices; its types are bus, star, mesh, tree and hybrid.
6.deeper:
A physical network diagram shows the actual physical arrangement of the components that make up the network, including cables and hardware, typically as a bird's eye view, like a floorplan. Physical topology refers to the physical interconnection of network devices. Bus: all the nodes connected by a central medium (the bus) with exactly two endpoints. Star: a central hub or switch through which all the data passes, with all the peripheral nodes connected to it. Mesh: in full mesh each node is directly connected to every other node; in partial mesh nodes are only connected to the nodes they interact with most. Tree: it combines characteristics of the bus and star topologies, with groups of star-configured workstations, called segments, connected to a linear bus backbone; it has a main trunk with multiple branches, like a tree.

Hybrid topology: most networks employ some combination of topologies, which yields what is called a hybrid topology.

Fiber optic: the physical diagram can show the type of cabling required, twisted pair or fiber optic. For twisted pair it shows which category, such as CAT5e or CAT 6; for fiber optic, whether it is single mode or multimode. Fiber optic cables have several different types of connectors.

TIA standards: each type of cable has a maximum distance it can be used without some type of signal degradation. TIA standards are utilized when developing these diagrams to ensure the proper cable type and distance is used, and connector types are covered in the TIA standards too.
6.analogy: Physical topology is like the floor plan of a building: it shows where every hallway and door actually is, not who walks through them.
6.scenario: An airman draws the physical diagram for a building. Each floor's workstations connect to their own switch in a star, and the switches hang off one bus backbone: a tree. A few routers in another room are fully meshed, so the whole network is a hybrid. The diagram also marks the fiber optic runs as single mode or multimode and follows TIA standards for cable type and distance.

6.summary: A bus topology is a physical topology in which all the nodes are connected by a central medium, the bus, which has exactly two endpoints.
6.deeper:
Physical topology refers to the physical interconnection of network devices, and the bus topology is one of its types. It is distinguished by having all the nodes connected by a central medium (the "bus") which has exactly two endpoints.

One of the most common topologies, the star topology consists of a central hub or switch, through which all the data passes, along with all the peripheral nodes connected to that central node.

6.summary: A logical network diagram describes the way information flows through a network; it typically shows subnets, network devices such as routers and firewalls, and routing protocols.
6.deeper:
A network diagram is a visual representation of a computer or telecommunications network; it can be either physical or logical. Logical network diagrams describe the way information flows through a network. Therefore they typically show subnets (including VLAN IDs, masks and addresses), network devices like routers and firewalls, and routing protocols.

In the OSI model, logical network diagrams correlate with the information contained in Layer 3 (L3). Also known as the "network layer", L3 is an abstraction layer that deals with packet forwarding through intermediate routers. Level 2 shows the data links between adjacent nodes, while level 1 shows the purely physical layout or topology.

IP addresses and subnets are laid out in logical network diagrams. This is useful when configuring the different network devices, and it is a handy reference for looking up IP addresses when troubleshooting a network. A logical diagram can also be a tool in evaluating network performance.
6.analogy: A logical network diagram is like a subway map: it shows the lines and stops and how to get from one to another, not where the tunnels actually run under the streets.
6.scenario: An airman troubleshoots a user who cannot reach a server. Instead of the floorplan of cables, the airman opens the logical network diagram, which shows the subnet with its VLAN ID, mask and addresses, the router and firewall in the path, and the routing protocol. It is a handy reference for looking up the IP addresses involved.
6.example: An organization chart shows who reports to whom, not where each desk sits. A logical network diagram shows how information flows, not where the cables run. In the course: Logical network diagrams describe the way information flows through a network, Block Text p.72.

6.summary: Logical topology is how information is passed through the network; unlike physical topology, it is bound to network protocols.
6.deeper:
Topology of a network refers to the way the network is connected and how it communicates; there are two types, physical topology and logical topology. Physical topology refers to the physical interconnection of network devices, such as bus, star, mesh and tree layouts.

Logical topology is how the information is passed through the network: the way the network operates, or how data travels or moves through it. The main difference from physical topology is that the logical topology is bound to network protocols. It is used to define the network architecture for data transfer across network nodes, to define the proper channel for data transfer, to maintain the network, and to create a path to send signals across it. Logical topology uses network protocols, which define the path for transferring packets; the most common example is the Ethernet protocol, which defines the logical path for communication of switches and nodes.

The logical topology can be used to design the network structure. It is considered a blueprint of the network, including all the nodes and switches and how the data will flow, and it can help implement the network physically in the physical topology. It is a high-level representation of a network. The logical and physical topology of a particular network may resemble one another, or they may be entirely different.
6.analogy: Physical topology is like the pipes in a building; logical topology is like the plan for which water goes to which tap. The plan follows rules of its own and need not look like the pipe layout.
6.scenario: An airman's network has every computer cabled to one central switch: its physical topology. The airman is asked how data moves across it. That answer depends on the network protocol in use, such as Ethernet, which defines the logical path between the switches and nodes: the logical topology.
6.example: A bus route map shows the order of stops a bus follows, while a street map shows how the streets are actually laid out. Logical topology is like the route map. In the course: The Logical Topology is how the information is passed through the network, Block Text p.73.

6.summary: Ethernet is the most common network protocol of a logical topology; it defines the logical path for switches and nodes and sends packets across the network.
6.deeper:
Logical topology uses network protocols, which define the path for transferring packets. The most common example of network protocols is the Ethernet protocol: it defines the logical path for communication of the different switches and nodes present in the network and sends packets across the network.

Ethernet is a contention-based network technology, meaning devices contend (or compete) for the right to transmit data. In an Ethernet environment all systems listen to the line or cable, waiting for an opportunity to gain access. If more than one device transmits at the same time, there will be a collision, and both devices will wait a random amount of time to retransmit.

Since only one system can be transmitting at any given time, Ethernet uses an access method or protocol known as Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection (CSMA/CD).
6.analogy: Ethernet is like a group of people sharing one microphone: everyone waits for a quiet moment, and if two grab it at once, both let go and each waits a moment before trying again.
6.scenario: Two computers on an Ethernet network have data to send. Each listens to the line and waits for an opportunity. Both start at the same moment and their transmissions collide. Both devices wait a random amount of time to retransmit.
6.example: At a four-way stop, cars take turns; if two start at once, both stop and wait before going again. Ethernet devices take turns on the line in a similar way. In the course: The most common example of network protocols is the Ethernet protocol, Block Text p.73.

6.term: Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection
6.summary: Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection (CSMA/CD) is a contention protocol that allows hosts to contend for network access; Ethernet uses it as its access method.
6.deeper:
Since only one system can be transmitting at any given time, Ethernet uses an access method or protocol known as Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection (CSMA/CD), a contention protocol that allows hosts to contend for network access. Broken down: CS, Carrier Sense: all devices listen before transmitting. MA, Multiple Access: multiple devices can access the network. CD, Collision Detection: rules to manage data collisions.

With CSMA/CD, all computers on the network (Multiple Access) check the cable for traffic (Carrier Sense) before attempting to transmit a frame of data. Data is sent only if the station does not "sense" any data being sent by other devices. Should two or more devices attempt to put data on the network, a collision occurs. How the devices detect the collision (Collision Detection) and how they respond to it is defined within the IEEE 802.3 rules of CSMA/CD.

CSMA/CD originates at the Data Link layer of the OSI reference model and is implemented at the Physical layer.
6.analogy: CSMA/CD is like people on a group phone call: everyone listens before speaking, anyone may speak, and if two start at once, both stop and try again.
6.scenario: Three computers share one cable. Before sending a frame, each one checks the cable for traffic. Two of them sense nothing and send at the same moment, and a collision occurs. The way they detect it and respond is set by the IEEE 802.3 rules of CSMA/CD.
6.example: If you and a friend both start talking at the same time, you each stop and then one of you speaks again. CSMA/CD manages a shared network the same way. In the course: CSMA/CD is defined as a contention protocol that allows hosts to contend for network access, Block Text p.74.

6.summary: A data flow diagram is a network representation of a system that uses four symbols to show data sources, destinations, flows, stores and transformations, with no decisions or timing.
6.deeper:
Data flow diagrams are a network representation of a system and the cornerstone for structured systems analysis and design. They use four symbols to represent any system at any level of detail. They do not show decisions or timing of events; their function is to illustrate data sources, destinations, flows, stores and transformations. Data flow diagrams present all possible paths: control, or how to select a specific path, is not shown, nor is repetition (how many times or when a procedure is performed), volumes, timing or frequency. A data flow diagram is like a road map: a network model of all possibilities, with no start or stop point and no timing, and different detail shown on different hierarchical levels ("leveling" or "partitioning").

External entities: sources or destinations outside the specified system boundary.

Data flows: the movement of data in the system. The data flows to and from the external entities shown on the context diagram all appear on the data flow diagram.

Processes: transforms of incoming data flow(s) to outgoing data flow(s).

Data stores, the fourth entity, are repositories for data that is not moving.
6.analogy: A data flow diagram is like a road map: it shows every road that exists, but not who drives where, when or how often.
6.scenario: An airman maps how data moves through a system. Users who send data in and offices that receive reports are drawn outside the system boundary as external entities. Arrows show the data flows, a process transforms incoming data into outgoing data, and a data store holds the data that is not moving. No arrow shows which path is chosen or when.
6.example: A road map of a state shows all the roads, and a city map shows more detail of one area, but neither shows traffic times. A data flow diagram shows paths for data the same way. In the course: Data flow diagrams are a network representation of a system, Block Text p.74.
